bio.en: Luc Levesque is the Chief Growth Officer at Shopify and was personally recruited by Mark Zuckerberg to help grow Facebook Messenger, Instagram, and WhatsApp; he previously served as VP of Growth and GM at Tripadvisor and has advised companies like Twitter, Pinterest, Patreon, Thumbtack, and Canva on growth.
bio.zh: Luc Levesque 是 Shopify 的首席增长官（Chief Growth Officer），曾被 Mark Zuckerberg 亲自招揽去推动 Facebook Messenger、Instagram 和 WhatsApp 的增长；他此前担任 Tripadvisor 的增长副总裁兼总经理，并曾为 Twitter、Pinterest、Patreon、Thumbtack 和 Canva 等公司提供增长顾问。

summary.en: Luc makes the case for hiring a great growth advisor, arguing that the right person at the right time can change a company's trajectory with a single sentence and deliver 100% to 1000%+ lifts. He shares how to decide when you need an advisor, how to structure the relationship, and what to look for in one. A large part of the conversation is devoted to SEO as a growth channel—who it suits, how to think about it, and how everything is about to change with AI tools like Bard and ChatGPT. He also offers unexpected advice on self-reflection, building routines, and cold plunges, plus memorable stories from working alongside Zuckerberg and the relentless 'impact' culture at Facebook.
summary.zh: Luc 力陈聘请一位优秀增长顾问的价值，他认为在对的时机遇到对的人，一句话就能改变公司的走向，带来 100% 乃至 1000% 以上的提升。他分享了如何判断自己是否需要顾问、如何设计合作关系，以及该看重顾问的哪些特质。对话的很大篇幅都集中在 SEO 这一增长渠道上——它适合谁、该怎么思考，以及随着 Bard、ChatGPT 这类 AI 工具出现，一切将如何改变。他还给出了关于自我反思、建立日常节奏和冷水浴的意外建议，并讲述了一些与 Zuckerberg 共事、以及 Facebook 那种对“影响力（impact）”近乎偏执的文化里的难忘故事。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: We talk about the 10X engineer and we don't really talk about the 10X growth advisor or 10X growth person, but the same dynamic applies. You could argue it applies even more because the right growth advisor can have literally company changing impact. Something I've experienced several times in hindsight when you're like, "Okay, here's the needle in the haystack." And then it's implemented and you can see hundreds of percentages, sometimes over a thousand percent lift when you get it right. It's one of those weird disciplines where the right person at the right time can literally say a sentence that changes the trajectory of your company. You can't say that for a lot of different disciplines, but this is one of them.
turns.zh: 我们谈论 10 倍工程师，而不是真正谈论 10 倍增长顾问或 10 倍增长人员，但同样的动态也适用。你可能会说它更适用，因为正确的成长顾问可以真正改变公司的影响。事后看来，我曾多次经历过这样的事情，当时你会说：“好吧，这是大海捞针。”然后实施后，如果正确的话，您可以看到数百％的提升，有时甚至超过一千％。这是一种奇怪的学科，正确的人在正确的时间可以说出一句话来改变公司的发展轨迹。对于许多不同的学科你不能这么说，但这就是其中之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Luc, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 卢克，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Thank you. Good to see you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。很高兴见到你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's good to see you too. I want to start with a story that you shared once when we were hanging out in the past and something that I'll never forget, and it's about the time that you just joined Facebook and apparently you had some kind of big presentation you had to give to the entire company or the executive staff. turns.zh: 很高兴见到你。我想从您过去在闲逛时分享的一个我永远不会忘记的故事开始，这是关于您刚刚加入 Facebook 的时候，显然您需要向整个公司或高管人员进行某种大型演示。然后我就是喜欢它的展开方式，它让你了解与扎克伯格以及在 Facebook 合作的感觉。如果这听起来很有趣，你能分享一下这个故事吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: If remember the story, well, basically I had just started at Facebook about... I'll use those two interchangeably. I remember it as Facebook and I always will. I was three months in and was working on a new area for me. So I came in, started putting together our thoughts on a strategy and was asked to do a presentation in front of the company with Mark on the strategy. So I whipped up a draft strategy, put together some plots and plans, presented in front of the company and went well. And then every six months there's something called the [inaudible 00:04:32] Team Review of Facebook and basically product area leads will go in and present their strategy, how it's going. Again, I just joined three months before, so I walk in no idea what to expect. I am sitting at a table. You can kind of envision it's a big room, a really big room with a bunch of tables set up in a big square with a little microphone.
turns.zh: 如果还记得这个故事，好吧，基本上我刚刚开始在 Facebook 工作……我会交替使用这两个。我记得它是 Facebook，而且永远都会。我在那里呆了三个月，正在为我的一个新领域工作。所以我进来了，开始整理我们对战略的想法，并被要求在公司面前与马克一起就该战略进行演示。因此，我起草了一份战略草案，整理了一些情节和计划，并向公司展示，进展顺利。然后，每六个月就会有一次所谓的 [听不清 00:04:32] Facebook 团队审核，基本上产品领域的负责人会介入并介绍他们的策略以及进展情况。再说一次，我三个月前才加入，所以我走进来时不知道会发生什么。我坐在一张桌子旁。你可以想象这是一个大房间，一个非常大的房间，在一个大广场上摆着一堆桌子，还有一个小麦克风。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So I sit in there, there's Mark and all the executives sitting on the other side. And I sit down and it's quiet for what felt like five minutes. I'm sure it was not, but it was quiet for a while, just sitting there waiting for what's going to happen now. And at some point Mark kind looks over, says, "Hey, we saw your presentation, saw your strategy. Now when are we going to start seeing results?" And that was my introduction to Facebook. It was kind of my introduction to working with Mark and was a pretty kind of intense thing to go through. Again, I just joined. The strategy was very much a draft at that point, but I think what it highlights is something that Facebook does really, really well, which you get very quickly when you join Facebook and it's why they're such an execution machine and can build a lot of great product. It's because they focus exclusively on that magic word, which is impact.
turns.zh: 所以我坐在那儿，马克和所有高管坐在另一边。我坐下来，感觉安静了大约五分钟。我确信不是，但它安静了一会儿，只是坐在那里等待现在要发生的事情。在某个时刻，马克·恩德看了过来，说道：“嘿，我们看到了您的演示，看到了您的策略。现在我们什么时候开始看到结果？”这就是我对 Facebook 的介绍。这是我与马克合作的开始，也是一件非常紧张的事情。再说一遍，我刚刚加入。当时该战略还只是一个草案，但我认为它强调的是 Facebook 做得非常非常好的事情，当你加入 Facebook 时你很快就能明白这一点，这就是为什么他们是这样一个执行机器，可以构建很多伟大的产品。这是因为他们只关注那个神奇的词，那就是影响力。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: And that was kind of my first introduction to working with Mark and just that laser focus on, "All right, got it. Now when are we going to start seeing impact and kind of moving from there?" So it's something that is very much in the culture there and something that is so important. It's something of course that we focus on a lot at Shopify, but it's that difference between, "I don't care how hard you've worked. I don't care what you're working on, what the activities are. What are the outcomes? What is the impact you're having?" I actually really love that word impact and focusing on it because it's vague enough that it covers off any work that is impactful towards the mission and it's precise enough to know what does that mean when you say, "Are you having impact? Or what is the impact we're having?" So it's a great way to approach things. That was my first experience there within a few months. And yeah, we jumped in and started focusing on having a lot of impact from there.
turns.zh: 这就是我与马克合作的第一次介绍，只是激光聚焦，“好吧，明白了。现在我们什么时候才能开始看到影响并从那里开始采取行动？”所以这是那里文化中非常重要的事情。当然，这是我们在 Shopify 非常关注的事情，但这就是“我不在乎你工作有多努力。我不在乎你在做什么，活动是什么。结果是什么？你产生的影响是什么？”之间的区别。事实上，我真的很喜欢“影响力”这个词，并专注于它，因为它足够模糊，它掩盖了任何对使命有影响力的工作，而且它足够精确，可以知道当你说“你有影响力吗？或者我们正在产生什么影响？”时这意味着什么？所以这是处理事情的好方法。这是我几个月内第一次在那里经历。是的，我们介入并开始专注于从那里产生很大的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that story. There's a couple things there. One is, if I were in your shoes, I'd poop my pants sitting there for five minutes waiting for what do you guys-
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个故事。那里有几件事。一是，如果我处于你们的处境，我会拉裤子坐在那里五分钟，等着你们做什么——

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: That did not happen. I had a report.
turns.zh: 但那并没有发生。我有一份报告。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. How did it go? How did you deal with it? Or I guess how did you respond?
turns.zh: 好的。进展如何？你是怎么处理的？或者我猜你是怎么回应的？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Well, we had, funny enough, already started having impact, so I was able to at least respond with, "Hey, we've kind of already started in a few ways" and walk through where we were having impact and just focus on the strategy, what our plans forward were and where we wanted to go from there. So I think that's how I responded.
turns.zh: 好吧，有趣的是，我们已经开始产生影响，所以我至少能够回应，“嘿，我们已经在一些方面开始了”，并介绍我们正在产生影响的地方，只关注战略、我们的未来计划是什么以及我们想要从那里走向何方。所以我想这就是我的回应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great work. So something I've started doing actually on this podcast is I've started to keep a little Post-it of, here it is, of themes that continue to recur across companies that are most successful. And impact comes... It's number one on my Post-it here, is just impact comes up so often as something that the best companies continue to come back to and focus on and put a lot of emphasis on. I guess I don't know what the question is exactly, but is that just what you find in the work that you do with all the companies you work with? Just how important it's to come back to impact as maybe the primary thing?
turns.zh: 好的，干得好。因此，我在这个播客上实际上开始做的事情是，我开始保留一些便利贴，这里就是那些在最成功的公司中不断重复出现的主题。影响力来了……这是我的便利贴上的第一名，只是影响力经常出现，最好的公司会继续回来关注并重点关注。我想我不知道问题到底是什么，但这就是你在与你合作的所有公司所做的工作中发现的吗？重新发挥影响力作为首要任务究竟有多重要？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think it's easy for a lot of leaders and companies to get caught up in how hard are people working, what did they do, and recognizing and rewarding activity. I mean, everybody wants to have impact. The companies that truly focus on that are the ones that break through and really make a lot of progress towards the mission. So that seems obvious I think when I say it out loud, but being in that culture and having it really ingrained in everything you do whether it's performance reviews or strategies or these reviews with the executive team, it all gravitates around impact. And I think it's that laser focus on it that matters so much. But I mean I've certainly seen it going other ways where it's more about working long hours. And certainly there's a correlation, to be clear, between working hard and impact, but I find it's just such a precise way to think about how people are performing or what you're doing in terms of is your strategy working? Is the direction you're moving in having the intended outcomes that you want? And yeah, I do think it's all about that.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，我认为很多领导者和公司很容易关注人们工作的努力程度、他们做了什么以及认可和奖励活动。我的意思是，每个人都想产生影响。真正专注于这一点的公司是那些能够突破并真正在实现使命方面取得很大进展的公司。因此，我认为当我大声说出来时，这似乎是显而易见的，但在这种文化中，并将其真正根植于你所做的每一件事中，无论是绩效评估、策略还是与执行团队的这些评估，这一切都围绕着影响力。我认为对它的高度关注才是最重要的。但我的意思是，我确实看到了其他方式，更多的是长时间工作。当然，需要明确的是，努力工作和影响力之间存在相关性，但我发现这是一种精确的方式来思考人们的表现或你正在做的事情是否有效？您前进的方向是否能达到您想要的预期结果？是的，我确实认为这就是全部。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Being a growth leader where everything's so measurable, impact is something that can be very clearly measured and you know whether you have it or not. So the most important thing that we work on constantly is reviewing what's our strategy, what are we working on? Is that driving towards the top level north star outcome we want? Is that having the impact? And then basically doing everything around that singular north star. So it's very, very important. I think it's more profound than it might seem just from the outside. But if you've worked in different companies, you've probably experienced different versions of this too.
turns.zh: 作为一个一切都可以衡量的增长领导者，影响力是可以非常清晰地衡量的，你知道自己是否拥有它。因此，我们不断努力的最重要的事情是回顾我们的战略是什么，我们正在做什么？这是否正在朝着我们想要的顶级北极星结果迈进？有这样的影响吗？然后基本上围绕那颗奇异的北极星做所有事情。所以这非常非常重要。我认为它比表面上看起来更深刻。但如果你在不同的公司工作过，你可能也经历过不同的版本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I want to spend more time on this, but before we move on, you also have another Zuck story. Correct me if I'm wrong, but Zuck recruited you personally to join Facebook/Meta. Is that true? And then if true, what was that like to be recruited by Zuck personally?
turns.zh: 是的。我想花更多的时间在这上面，但在我们继续之前，你还有另一个扎克的故事。如果我错了，请纠正我，但扎克亲自招募你加入 Facebook/Meta。这是真的吗？如果这是真的，被扎克亲自招募是什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: It was an interesting experience, very intense, but also one of the reasons for it was I was living in Canada and my family was there and I had some strong personal reasons why I couldn't leave Canada. But yeah, we had a lot of discussions with Mark. I won't get into the micro details of it, that's more Mark's story to tell than mine. But a few takeaways from going through that experience. As a leader, hiring is the most important thing as we all know. It's a craft and a skill that I'm always working on refining. I have my own playbook that I'm constantly tweaking, testing out different approaches, trying to find the best talent and assessing them and trying to close them and bringing them on board. So I learned a lot through that experience with Mark.
turns.zh: 这是一次有趣的经历，非常激烈，但也是原因之一是我住在加拿大，我的家人在那里，我有一些强烈的个人原因为什么我不能离开加拿大。但是，是的，我们与马克进行了很多讨论。我不会深入讨论它的微观细节，这更多是马克的故事而不是我的故事。但从这次经历中我们得到了一些收获。众所周知，作为领导者，招聘是最重要的事情。这是我一直在努力完善的一门手艺和一项技能。我有自己的剧本，我会不断调整，测试不同的方法，试图找到最好的人才并评估他们，并试图吸引他们并让他们加入。所以我通过与马克的经历学到了很多东西。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: A couple things that stood out were the first one would be that Mark really involved the entire executive team. It wasn't just me talking to recruiting or talent or HR or just Mark, it was the entire executive team. That's something that I think a lot of leaders don't take advantage of. I've seen leaders, I've certainly done this at times where you go it alone or you're working with recruiting, but the reality is all the leaders, all the execs in the company know how important it's to bring in talent and they're always more than happy to help. So that's something that I think more leaders should do is really recruit all of their peers and their leaders in the company to help close. And that's certainly something that happened when I was in discussions with Mark and Facebook about joining.
turns.zh: 值得注意的几件事是，第一件事是马克真正让整个执行团队参与其中。不仅仅是我在与招聘、人才、人力资源或马克交谈，还有整个管理团队。我认为很多领导者都没有利用这一点。我见过领导者，有时我会单独行动或负责招聘，但现实是所有领导者、公司所有高管都知道引进人才的重要性，而且他们总是非常乐意提供帮助。因此，我认为更多的领导者应该做的就是真正招募公司中的所有同事和领导者来帮助完成任务。这肯定是我与 Mark 和 Facebook 讨论加入事宜时发生的事情。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: The second one, which I had I suppose never experienced before, was that they made it very personal. I had these reasons why I couldn't leave. So initially I was excited by the opportunity, but I couldn't see myself moving to California for personal reasons. And through discussions, Mark basically involved my wife, involved my spouse in this, Andrea. We flew down, had dinner with him and Priscilla, his wife. Andrea had ended up meeting with many of the executives at Facebook and really talking through what was holding us back, why we couldn't come, potential options and ideas for how we could come down.
turns.zh: 第二个，我想我以前从未经历过，是他们把它变得非常个性化。我有这些理由让我无法离开。因此，最初我对这个机会感到很兴奋，但由于个人原因，我不认为自己会搬到加利福尼亚。通过讨论，马克基本上让我的妻子、我的配偶安德里亚也参与其中。我们飞下来，与他和他的妻子普里西拉共进晚餐。安德里亚最终与 Facebook 的许多高管进行了会面，并真正讨论了阻碍我们前进的因素、我们不能来的原因、潜在的选择以及我们如何解决问题的想法。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: But involving somebody's spouse and family I think is a really good idea because it's a very personal decision to change company. It involves more than just that person you're talking to, it involves the whole family. So that was something that I think is an important thing to have in your kind of playbook for hiring, is really think about the whole person's family and involve them if you can. In fact, Toby did this as well at Shopify. He flew down here with Fiona and we had breakfast with Andrea and them and reviewed a few offers when I joined Shopify.
turns.zh: 但我认为让某人的配偶和家人参与进来是一个非常好的主意，因为更换公司是一个非常个人的决定。它不仅仅涉及与你交谈的那个人，还涉及整个家庭。因此，我认为，在招聘手册中，这一点非常重要，真正考虑到整个人的家庭，并尽可能让他们参与进来。事实上，Toby 在 Shopify 也这么做了。他和 Fiona 一起飞到这里，我们和 Andrea 以及他们一起吃早餐，并在我加入 Shopify 时查看了一些优惠。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: And then the third thing is just to be absolutely relentless and don't give up and don't let momentum drop. It took seven months for me to go from, "This is amazing, exciting, but there's no way I can make this work" to, "Okay, let's move to Palo Alto." And Mark, the execs, a variety of leaders there were in discussions for months and months and months and never letting the momentum die. That's something that I think is really important. No doesn't necessarily mean no, and in this case it definitely wasn't the case. I had the same experience with Toby at Shopify where we've been talking about working together for over 10 years now. And then finally the timing was right and I was able to join the company.
turns.zh: 第三件事就是要绝对坚持不懈，不要放弃，不要让动力下降。我花了七个月的时间才从“这太棒了，令人兴奋，但我无法完成这项工作”到“好吧，我们搬到帕洛阿尔托吧”。马克、高管们以及各种领导人进行了数月的讨论，并且从未让这种势头消退。我认为这非常重要。 “不”并不一定意味着“不”，在这种情况下，情况绝对不是这样。我和 Shopify 的 Toby 也有过同样的经历，我们已经谈论了 10 多年的合作。最后时机成熟，我得以加入这家公司。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So just be relentless, involve the family, involve the spouse if you can, and recruit some help from other executives in the company. Those were some of the things that stood out through my experience. But yeah, it was a pretty wild time in my life.
turns.zh: 因此，要坚持不懈，让家人参与进来，如果可以的话让配偶参与进来，并向公司其他高管寻求帮助。这些是我的经历中突出的一些事情。但是，是的，那是我生命中一段非常疯狂的时光。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Relentless is actually another word. I wasn't necessarily I'm supposed to yet, but I feel like it's another trend to cross. The most impactful and successful founders is just this like, "I will not give up. I will keep at it."
turns.zh: 无情实际上是另一个词。我还不一定应该这样做，但我觉得这是另一种需要跨越的趋势。最有影响力和最成功的创始人就是这样的，“我不会放弃。我会坚持下去。”

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: [inaudible 00:13:10].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so that's a really interesting example of that in action. I was going to talk about this later, but maybe it's a good time to talk about it now, which is around hiring. So you talked about you have this playbook for how to hire. You mentioned to me that you kind of find that as you scale as a leader, hiring ends up being like the most important skill maybe, maybe one of the most important skills. I'd love to hear your take on just what you found about hiring as you've grown as a product leader.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常有趣的实际例子。我本来打算稍后再讨论这个问题，但也许现在是讨论这个问题的好时机，因为这是关于招聘的。所以你谈到你有一本关于如何招聘的手册。您向我提到，您发现，随着您成为领导者，招聘最终可能成为最重要的技能，也许是最重要的技能之一。我很想听听您在成长为产品领导者过程中对招聘的看法。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Well, I think you reach a point in your career where you realize that hiring is the skill you now need to become world-class at because you're not no longer doing the work yourself. You're still of course involved and doing some of the work and getting your hands dirty, but the bulk of your team's success now will be the quality of the hires you make and you truly need to be world-class at that. So yeah, I built this playbook out. I was in Canada in Ottawa when I sold that company, Tripadvisor, and really started growing my team and becoming more Leaning into leadership at the time through that experience.
turns.zh: 好吧，我认为你在职业生涯中达到了一个阶段，你意识到招聘是你现在成为世界一流的技能，因为你不再需要自己做这项工作。当然，你仍然会参与其中，做一些工作并亲自动手，但你的团队现在的成功大部分将取决于你所聘用的员工的质量，而你确实需要在这方面达到世界一流的水平。是的，我编写了这本剧本。当我出售 Tripadvisor 公司时，我正在加拿大渥太华，并通过这段经历真正开始发展我的团队，并变得更加倾向于当时的领导力。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: One of the benefits of being in Ottawa and kind of off the grid if you will, is it's a curse and a benefit as that you don't have a ton of people you can learn from. So it does mean you need to go to first principles and think things through from the ground up. It takes a little longer, but you come up with your own playbooks on how to do things. I think you've seen my blueprint, which is a good example of that where I have this blueprint I put together. When new people join the team, I show them my blueprint, which is basically a list of my quirks so we can really quickly align. That's something that just being in Ottawa and trying to figure out how to be a leader and avoid mistakes, I was like, "Wouldn't it be nice if you had a blueprint? When somebody joined, you can just tell them all of your quirks and you can just quickly calibrate on how it is to work together versus through awkward long discussions over the course of a year."
turns.zh: 在渥太华的好处之一是，如果你愿意的话，有点脱离电网，这是一种诅咒，也是一种好处，因为你没有很多可以向你学习的人。因此，这确实意味着您需要遵循首要原则并从头开始思考问题。这需要更长的时间，但你会想出自己的做事手册。我想你已经看到了我的蓝图，这是我整理的蓝图的一个很好的例子。当新人加入团队时，我会向他们展示我的蓝图，这基本上是我的怪癖列表，这样我们就可以真正快速地协调一致。这就是在渥太华并试图找出如何成为领导者并避免错误的事情，我想，“如果你有一个蓝图不是很好吗？当有人加入时，你可以告诉他们你所有的怪癖，你可以快速调整如何一起工作，而不是在一年的时间里通过尴尬的长时间讨论。”

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: My hiring playbook's a similar thing. I think of it in three different chapters, if you will. There's finding talent, assessing talent, and closing talent. In terms of finding talent, I do believe that the best predictor of future performance is past performance. So I'm looking for what I call signs of excellence. So I want to know the top people generally have done multiple amazing things in their life, repeated success, not just once. Maybe it was work related, maybe not work related. But generally speaking, if you think back to the stars you've worked with, they've done some amazing things. And that's why I always start when I interview or when I chat with people, I started talking about just trying to understand, "What has been your path? What have you done professionally and not professionally?" And generally, stars going to stand out. It's very rare that there's not something obvious that comes through.
turns.zh: 我的招聘手册也是类似的事情。如果你愿意的话，我会在三个不同的章节中思考它。包括发现人才、评估人才和关闭人才。在寻找人才方面，我确实相信未来绩效的最佳预测因素是过去的绩效。所以我正在寻找我所说的卓越标志。所以我想知道顶尖的人在他们的一生中一般都做过很多令人惊奇的事情，屡次成功，而不仅仅是一次。也许与工作有关，也许与工作无关。但总的来说，如果你回想一下与你合作过的明星，他们做了一些令人惊奇的事情。这就是为什么当我采访或与人聊天时，我总是开始谈论只是试图理解，“你的道路是什么？你专业地做了什么，不专业地做了什么？”一般来说，明星都会脱颖而出。很少有没有明显的事情发生。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So for myself personally, I'm looking for kind of three different signs of excellence to tell me that it doesn't have to be three. The mental model I have is as you're talking to them, you're getting pluses and negatives. There's red flags you're hearing and there's really great things. And then at the end you can make an opinion of how good this person is.
turns.zh: 因此，就我个人而言，我正在寻找三种不同的卓越标志来告诉我，它不一定是三个。我的思维模式是，当你与他们交谈时，你会得到优点和缺点。你会听到一些危险信号，但也有一些非常棒的事情。最后你可以对这个人的优秀程度做出评价。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Another great sign of excellence, and this was just through reflecting on stars on the team and thinking what makes them unique, what about them. One of them is when somebody's boss leaves the company and then comes back to poach them, that is such a strong signal because if you think of what just happened, the leader who knows exactly how good this person you're talking to is, they have the most knowledge of the performance of this individual, they left the company. They've come back to poach them, putting their own reputation at risk by coming back depending on the situation. And they would never do that unless this person was really, really good.
turns.zh: 卓越的另一个重要标志，这只是通过反思团队中的明星并思考他们的独特之处以及他们的特点。其中之一是当某人的老板离开公司然后回来挖走他们时，这是一个非常强烈的信号，因为如果你想想刚刚发生的事情，领导者确切地知道与你交谈的这个人有多优秀，他们最了解这个人的表现，他们离开了公司。他们回来挖走他们，视情况回来，将自己的声誉置于危险之中。除非这个人真的非常非常好，否则他们永远不会这样做。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So you don't want to over pivot on one signal, you want to look at the full picture. But those are the types of things I look at to bring in top talent. And I've got this whole playbook, mistakes I've made that I've learned from, things to avoid. And over the years, yeah, I've put together this playbook that I try to follow and I'm always running little experiments to try to make it better.
turns.zh: 因此，您不想过度关注一个信号，而是想查看整个情况。但这些正是我所关注的引进顶尖人才的方式。我有这整本剧本，我犯过的错误，我从中吸取了教训，以及要避免的事情。多年来，是的，我已经整理了这本我试图遵循的剧本，并且我总是进行一些小实验以尝试使其变得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Were going to that blueprint that you mentioned. A lot of which you're talking about is probably more relevant to senior executive type people because you're looking for... Or maybe not because you're looking for say three.
turns.zh: 我们要去你提到的那个蓝图。您所谈论的很多内容可能与高级管理人员类型的人更相关，因为您正在寻找……或者可能不是，因为您正在寻找三个。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: [inaudible 00:17:06].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So people early in their career could also have three, say, moments of excellence?
turns.zh: 好的。那么，职业生涯早期的人也可能拥有三个卓越时刻？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I mean just thinking off the top, it depends on the type of person you're hiring, but are they a founder? Have they tried to do something? Did they win an award somewhere? Are they a gold medalist at something? Have they done something that others have not that shows grit, that shows drive, that shows the ability to succeed? And I've seen that you can apply that to any candidate you're hiring.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是从顶层考虑，这取决于你雇用的人的类型，但他们是创始人吗？他们尝试过做某事吗？他们在某个地方获奖了吗？他们是某方面的金牌得主吗？他们是否做了别人没有做过的事情，显示出勇气、显示出干劲、显示出成功的能力？我发现你可以将这一点应用到你正在招聘的任何候选人身上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The implication there is, without that, they're probably not going to be stars, that there's a strong correlation between having signs of excellence and them performing really well in this role.
turns.zh: 这意味着，如果没有这一点，他们可能不会成为明星，拥有卓越的迹象和他们在这个角色中表现出色之间存在很强的相关性。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Correct, exactly. Yeah, I mean I suppose it's possible, but it would be pretty rare that somebody would come in without some sign that they stand above the crowd. And again, I'm talking about you generally want to hire the top 1% of candidates. So when you're looking for the best of the best, you definitely are looking for those signals.
turns.zh: 正确，完全正确。是的，我的意思是我认为这是可能的，但是很少有人进来时没有任何迹象表明他们站在人群之上。再说一遍，我说的是，您通常希望聘用排名前 1% 的候选人。因此，当您寻找最好的产品时，您肯定会寻找这些信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so I'm going to bring us back on the agenda that I had for myself, which is I want to start with talking about advisorships and advising and growth advisors. You've been a growth advisor for a long time to some of the most amazing companies out there, Twitter, Pinterest, Patreon, Canva, Thumbtack. I'm sure there's others that you don't list that are more informal. Now you work at Shopify. And so what I think about here is a lot of founders often think about, "Should I bring on an advisor? What should I look for an advisor? I've heard stories of advisors being useless sometimes. People tell me I don't need advisors." So I guess the question here is just what's your take on when it makes sense to bring on and consider bringing on a growth advisor and what should people look for when they're exploring and talking to a potential growth advisor?
turns.zh: 惊人的。好的，我要回到我自己的议程上来，我想从谈论顾问、建议和成长顾问开始。您长期以来一直担任一些最出色的公司的增长顾问，例如 Twitter、Pinterest、Patreon、Canva、Thumbtack。我确信您还没有列出其他更非正式的内容。现在您在 Shopify 工作。因此，我在这里想到的是很多创始人经常思考的问题：“我应该聘请顾问吗？我应该寻找顾问做什么？我听说过顾问有时毫无用处的故事。人们告诉我，我不需要顾问。”所以我想这里的问题是，当聘请和考虑聘请一名成长顾问有意义时，您的看法是什么？人们在探索和与潜在的成长顾问交谈时应该寻找什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: A few thoughts. In terms of when, I don't think you can probably come into early. It's probably harder to find really good ones than it is to time it. But generally speaking, I would say you don't want to focus too much on growth until you have product market fit. So make sure you have a product that users love that's either showing strong signs of retention or has some good loop that you can see that you can start thinking about growth.
turns.zh: 一些想法。至于什么时候，我认为你可能无法提前进入。找到真正好的产品可能比把握时机更难。但一般来说，我想说，在产品适合市场之前，你不想过多关注增长。因此，请确保您拥有一款用户喜欢的产品，该产品要么表现出强烈的保留迹象，要么具有良好的循环，您可以看到您可以开始考虑增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me follow on that thread real quick because I find some founders still want to have someone come help them with growth even though they know they don't have product market fit, even though this tip comes up every single time when I'm talking to growth person, like, "Wait till you have product market fit before doing growth stuff." So could you just add a little bit of why that's important while we're on that topic?
turns.zh: 让我快速跟进这个话题，因为我发现一些创始人仍然希望有人来帮助他们实现增长，即使他们知道自己没有产品市场契合度，尽管每次我与增长人员交谈时都会出现这个提示，比如“等到产品市场契合后再做增长的事情。”那么您能否补充一点为什么在我们讨论该主题时这一点很重要？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Growth advice is generally always applicable. And if you can start thinking about how to build your product early, even if it's pre-product market fit, you're not going to do any damage, but you may be wasting some capital on an advisor or a growth person too early. The problem that I see is if you start growing a product that doesn't have product market fit, you're actually doing more damage than good because you have a product that is now being exposed to the market through growth levers and through optimization that is giving a bad experience with your product. And you want that product that you know is tight and you know has product market fit to start building the flywheel and start growing. You don't want it to be growing if it doesn't satisfy that need that you're trying to build out for. So I can see it having more damage than good because when somebody tries something, they're unlikely to try it again. And so that's the dangerous game you can get into. So you're better off with a good product that's satisfying a need and then growing from there.
turns.zh: 成长建议通常总是适用的。如果您可以尽早开始考虑如何构建您的产品，即使它是产品前的市场契合度，您也不会造成任何损害，但您可能会过早地在顾问或成长人员上浪费一些资本。我看到的问题是，如果你开始开发一款不适合产品市场的产品，那么你实际上弊大于利，因为你的产品现在通过增长杠杆和优化暴露在市场上，这会给你的产品带来糟糕的体验。你想要那种你知道是紧张的产品，你知道它有适合市场的产品来开始构建飞轮并开始增长。如果它不能满足您试图构建的需求，您就不希望它增长。所以我可以看到它的弊大于利，因为当有人尝试某件事时，他们不太可能再尝试一次。这就是你可能参与的危险游戏。因此，您最好拥有一款能够满足需求并以此为基础不断发展的好产品。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I will say to kind of play devil's advocate with myself and something that I've done actually in one of the products, I've built several consumer products and grown them, is that sometimes to know if you have a product, you need users to use it. So there's like some subtlety in here, but I would say if you are trying to get users in to start playing with it at scale, I mean try to focus in on a market that is maybe off the grid. Like pick some English-speaking country that's a bit off the grid that you can isolate your marketing to so you can start getting dozens or a couple hundred people per day coming in and giving you feedback.
turns.zh: 我会说，对自己来说有点唱反调，我在其中一个产品中实际上做了一些事情，我已经构建了几种消费产品并发展了它们，有时要知道你是否有一个产品，你需要用户使用它。所以这里有一些微妙之处，但我想说，如果你试图让用户开始大规模使用它，我的意思是尝试专注于可能脱离电网的市场。比如选择一些有点脱离电网的英语国家，你可以将你的营销隔离到其中，这样你就可以开始每天有几十或几百人进来给你反馈。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I've seen that work too. So I'd say wait till you have product market fit. If you do start growing your product early because you need that signal from people actually using it beyond just focus groups and friends or small numbers of people, try to do it off the grid in smaller markets that you can get kind of contain the growth and get what you're really trying to get, which is that signal on is it working or not.
turns.zh: 我也看过那个作品。所以我想说等到你的产品适合市场。如果你确实很早就开始发展你的产品，因为你需要来自实际使用它的人的信号，而不仅仅是焦点小组和朋友或少数人，那么尝试在较小的市场中脱离电网，你可以得到某种程度的控制增长并得到你真正想要得到的东西，这就是它是否有效的信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, I threw us off track. Let's get back on track. So we're talking about when it makes sense to find a growth advisor and then what to look for and so on that you might want to work with.
turns.zh: 惊人的。好吧，我让我们偏离了轨道。让我们回到正轨吧。因此，我们讨论的是何时寻找成长顾问有意义，然后是寻找什么，等等您可能想与之合作的问题。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I mean, what makes a great growth advisor is somebody who really understands what to do but also why certain growth levers work. It's that kind of deep understanding of levers of onboarding or whatever area they're focusing on that really makes growth advisor stand out. So when you're looking for a growth advisor, you want to have those discussions to see like, "How much depth does this person have? Have they seen a playbook and they're just good at repeating the playbook or are they evolving, are they growing?" The best way to get to know that is to start really asking them questions about growth and growth advising and the certain things that they've done and why they think those have worked.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，成为一名优秀的增长顾问的关键是真正了解该做什么以及某些增长杠杆为何有效。正是对入职杠杆或他们所关注的任何领域的深刻理解才真正使增长顾问脱颖而出。因此，当你在寻找成长顾问时，你希望进行这样的讨论：“这个人有多少深度？他们是否看过剧本并且他们只是擅长重复剧本，或者他们是否正在进化，他们是否正在成长？”了解这一点的最好方法是开始真正向他们询问有关增长和增长建议的问题，以及他们所做的某些事情以及为什么他们认为这些事情有效。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: This can be tricky if you don't yourself know growth. So I think one thing that I have not seen a lot of founders do that I would advise is if you have an advisor already... Because this applies to finding growth advisors, but it also applies to hiring good growth talent. So if you have somebody you know whether it's already an advisor or somebody who knows growth, you can solicit their help in trying to flesh out whether somebody you're trying to hire is of high talent. So if you have an advisor, you can make that one of their roles is vet out any new talent coming in. And if you're looking for an advisor, try to find somebody that you know and trust who can do that first pass. Because for somebody who knows growth that you trust, it's actually not a lot of work for them to vet out how talented someone else's. It's an easy ask to make and something that if you have that person in your network or that worked with you that you can leverage for.
turns.zh: 如果您自己不了解增长，这可能会很棘手。所以我认为我没有看到很多创始人做的一件事是，我建议你是否已经有一名顾问……因为这适用于寻找成长顾问，但它也适用于雇用优秀的成长人才。因此，如果你有认识的人，无论他已经是顾问还是了解成长的人，你都可以寻求他们的帮助，以确定你要雇用的人是否具有高素质。因此，如果您有顾问，您可以让他们的角色之一是审查任何新加入的人才。如果您正在寻找顾问，请尝试找到您认识并信任的可以完成第一关的人。因为对于那些你信任的了解成长的人来说，他们实际上不需要做很多工作来审查别人的才华。这是一个很容易提出的要求，如果你的网络中有那个人或者与你一起工作的人，你就可以利用这个人。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: But I haven't seen that too often where founders kind of take advantage of people they know or existing growth advisors to help recruit and vet talent because it can be quite hard if you don't know the growth space to know if somebody's good or not.
turns.zh: 但我并没有经常看到创始人利用他们认识的人或现有的成长顾问来帮助招聘和审查人才，因为如果你不知道成长空间，就很难知道某人是否优秀。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really interesting idea and it could be where you find someone that's too busy to work with you, but maybe you could just ask, "Hey, could you just easily help me vet people?" And it takes a lot less time.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常有趣的想法，你可能会发现某个人太忙而无法与你一起工作，但也许你可以问，“嘿，你能轻松地帮助我审查人员吗？”而且花费的时间要少得多。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I've never been asked that, which is, I mean I don't know if I'll start getting asked this now, but it does seem like that's a really simple way to add a ton of value. And as a founder, I mean even if you have to pay this person or whatever you have to do, but it's such an important hire to get right. We talk about the 10X engineer and we don't really talk about the 10X growth advisor or 10X growth person, but the same dynamic applies. You could argue it applies even more because the right growth advisor can have literally company changing impact where they're either building or helping to ideate or helping to implement a growth loop that literally changes the company. As we know, you need a great product and you need a great growth loop. And it's usually just one loop that you need to get right. Most companies have gotten to where they are just off of one really strong channel that they've just dominated, so it's important to get right.
turns.zh: 是的，我从来没有被问过这个问题，也就是说，我不知道我现在是否会开始被问到这个问题，但这似乎是一种增加大量价值的非常简单的方法。作为一名创始人，我的意思是，即使你必须付钱给这个人或做任何你必须做的事情，但这是一个非常重要的招聘。我们谈论 10 倍工程师，而不是真正谈论 10 倍增长顾问或 10 倍增长人员，但同样的动态也适用。你可能会说它更适用，因为合适的增长顾问可以对公司产生真正的改变影响，他们可以构建或帮助构思或帮助实施真正改变公司的增长循环。众所周知，您需要出色的产品，并且需要良好的增长循环。通常您只需要完成一个循环即可。大多数公司已经到达了他们刚刚占据主导地位的一个非常强大的渠道，因此正确的做法很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that sort of impact that you've seen in your advisorship or other people's of just an impact from one conversation or a little bit of a help?
turns.zh: 您在您的顾问或其他人的顾问中是否看到过一次谈话或一点点帮助所产生的影响的例子？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Definitely. And I think what I would point to is the advantage of a growth advisor is it takes a long time to understand a channel. Certainly people have to know their stuff, they have to be very good at their craft, their growth craft, but also they have to be exposed to a large set of experiments or an environment where they've just seen what works and what doesn't. So no matter how good somebody is, if they haven't been exposed to an environment where there's a lot of experimentation, a lot of learning, it's very hard for them to internalize that. So once a growth advisor has that, it's takes years to learn it, but it literally can take seconds literally to communicate that. So I've worked with some companies that you've mentioned and certainly have had impact very quickly.
turns.zh: 确实。我想我要指出的是增长顾问的优势是需要很长时间才能了解渠道。当然，人们必须了解他们的东西，他们必须非常擅长他们的技巧，他们的成长技巧，但他们也必须接触大量的实验或环境，在那里他们刚刚看到什么有效，什么无效。因此，无论一个人有多优秀，如果他们没有接触过一个有大量实验、大量学习的环境，他们就很难内化这些。因此，一旦成长顾问掌握了这一点，就需要花费数年的时间来学习它，但实际上可能只需要几秒钟的时间来传达这一点。我曾与你提到的一些公司合作过，并且很快就产生了影响。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I mean, one example would be a company that I worked with. Now, a public company. At the time, they weren't. On day one, walked in, they presented their strategy, their plans, their funnels and their landing pages. I could see very quickly that there was something they were doing that was a little off and I asked them, "Well, why are you doing it that way?" And they said, "Well, we think it just looks better that way." And I said, "Well, just do it this other way." I remember this because it was such a short conversation and then three weeks later we connected and I heard they had rolled it out and it was a large impact that they had from this one change. This has happened many times with the companies I've worked with, but it's a good example that once you know it, it's not hard to recognize it if you deeply understand it to give advice, but it takes a long time to get the base knowledge.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我曾合作过的一家公司就是一个例子。现在是上市公司。当时，他们不是。第一天，他们走进来，展示了他们的策略、计划、渠道和登陆页面。我很快就发现他们正在做的事情有点不对劲，我问他们：“那么，你们为什么要这样做呢？”他们说：“好吧，我们认为这样看起来更好。”我说：“好吧，就用别的方法吧。”我记得这一点是因为这是一次简短的谈话，三周后我们联系上了，我听说他们已经推出了它，这一变化对他们产生了巨大的影响。这种情况在我合作过的公司里已经发生过很多次了，但这是一个很好的例子，一旦你了解了它，如果你深入了解它并给出建议，就不难识别它，但需要很长时间才能获得基础知识。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So I don't do these too often anymore, but when I do advise, I take them very seriously. I focus exclusively on having impact. I think that's really important because like you say, there's a lot of advisors out there. Some of them are great, some of them different qualities, and you really want to make sure that if you are an advisor, you want to be in the camp of when this person comes in, they have a lot of impact and it takes time and focus and energy and alignment and there's a bunch of things we can talk about that that helps to drive that alignment. But having impact is the most important thing, whether you're an advisor or if you're hiring because it's one of those weird disciplines where the right person at the right time can literally say a sentence that changes the trajectory of your company. You can't say that for a lot of different disciplines, but this is one of them.
turns.zh: 所以我不再经常这样做，但当我提出建议时，我会非常认真地对待它们。我只专注于产生影响力。我认为这非常重要，因为就像你说的，那里有很多顾问。他们中的一些人很棒，一些人的素质不同，你真的想确保，如果你是一名顾问，当这个人进来时你想加入其中，他们有很大的影响力，这需要时间、专注、精力和协调，我们可以谈论很多事情来帮助推动这种协调。但无论你是顾问还是招聘人员，影响力都是最重要的，因为这是一种奇怪的学科，在正确的时间正确的人可以说一句话改变你公司的发展轨迹。对于许多不同的学科你不能这么说，但这就是其中之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's that word impact again,
turns.zh: 又是这个词的冲击力

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Impact. Impact.
turns.zh: 影响。影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The point you just made about how one conversation can have a ton of impact is a reminder of why sometimes the price of an advisor feels absurd where like, "For one hour it's like thousands of dollars," but it's because obviously they spent a decade learning a thing and one conversation is all of that work they put into it crystallized for you in the moment.
turns.zh: 你刚才提出的关于一次对话如何产生巨大影响的观点提醒我们，为什么有时顾问的价格感觉很荒谬，比如“一小时就像数千美元”，但这是因为显然他们花了十年的时间来学习一件事，而一次对话是他们在此刻为你投入的所有工作的结晶。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Exactly. It's something I've experienced several times in hindsight when you're like, "Okay, here's the needle in the haystack" and then it's implemented and you can see hundreds of percentages, sometimes over a thousand percent lift when you get it right. It's exhilarating. It's great. I have something I used to say, which is, you want your impact to be so big there's a slide in the next board deck on try to explain what happened. That can happen when you are advising companies because you're able to share a very quickly insights. But one way to drive alignment is not everybody can do this, not all advisors do it this way, but I personally love just when I do these, which is not that frequent, just purely doing equity because I love the alignment in outcomes where the founder will be successful and you will be successful. So the incentives are really good to drive the right performance and the right outcomes that you want as a founder.
turns.zh: 确切地。这是我事后多次经历过的事情，当你想，“好吧，这是大海捞针”，然后它被实施，你可以看到数百个百分比，有时超过一千个百分点的提升，如果你做对了。真是令人兴奋。这很棒。我曾经说过一句话，那就是，你希望自己的影响力如此之大，以致于下一张董事会上有一张幻灯片试图解释发生了什么。当您为公司提供咨询时，这种情况就会发生，因为您能够非常快速地分享见解。但推动一致性的一种方法不是每个人都能做到这一点，并非所有顾问都这样做，但我个人喜欢我这样做，这并不常见，只是纯粹做股权，因为我喜欢结果的一致性，创始人会成功，你也会成功。因此，激励措施确实可以很好地推动创始人所希望的正确绩效和正确结果。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So if you can do it, I would definitely advise founders to bring advisors in for equity if you can. I think the same applies for your internal growth team. You want to make sure that the teams are incentivized not on activities, on doing stuff, because there's a lot of stuff to be done in growth, but really driving the outcomes that you want. And equity's just a great way of saying, "Hey, we're in this together. We're on the same side of the table. Let's go grow this company."
turns.zh: 因此，如果你能做到的话，我绝对会建议创始人聘请顾问以获得股权。我认为这同样适用于您的内部增长团队。你要确保团队的激励不是在活动上、在做事上，因为在增长过程中有很多事情要做，而是真正推动你想要的结果。股权只是一种很好的表达方式：“嘿，我们在一起。我们站在谈判桌的同一边。让我们一起发展这家公司。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was actually about to ask you what kind of structure you recommend for an advisorship. Is there anything else you can share about just what you'd recommend a founder do in terms of compensation for an advisor?
turns.zh: 我实际上想问你推荐什么样的顾问结构。关于您建议创始人在顾问薪酬方面采取的措施，您还有什么可以分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: There's a couple things. I'm a big fan of equity because of the alignment of incentives. You should think about, without getting into too much detail of the actual structure of the deals, but think about how you vest the equity. The last thing you want is an advisor holding back on sharing knowledge. The ideal engagement would be an advisor comes in, delivers as much value as possible quickly, and then trains your team. And then maybe it's a one-year engagement and hopefully they've learned because the advisor has been incentivized to share as much as possible and to train the team as much as possible. And then ideally you don't need them anymore after. So there's something there about structuring equity vesting. I'm a big fan of vesting earlier rather than later. So think about in terms of structure you're vesting, commensurate with the value you want, which is very much front loaded.
turns.zh: 有几件事。由于激励措施的一致性，我非常喜欢股权。你应该考虑一下，但不要过多考虑交易的实际结构，而是考虑如何归属股权。您最不想要的就是顾问拒绝分享知识。理想的参与是顾问介入，快速提供尽可能多的价值，然后培训您的团队。然后也许这是为期一年的参与，希望他们已经学到了东西，因为顾问被激励去尽可能多地分享并尽可能多地培训团队。理想情况下，您之后就不再需要它们了。因此，存在一些关于构建股权归属的问题。我非常喜欢尽早兑现而不是推迟兑现。因此，请考虑您所授予的结构，与您想要的价值相称，这是非常预先加载的。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I'm also a big fan of three month cliffs. Something I've done, I always do actually, is listen, in the first three months you'll know both sides if it's working or not. And you want to de-risk that on both sides because it really should be seen as a partnership between the advisor and the founder. If the founder thinks you're not adding value in the first few months, I think they should just tear it up and both sides move on. It's not good for the founder to continue the deal and it's not good frankly for the advisor because they're not, for some reason, able to add value in that environment. So I love a three-month cliff at the beginning where if it's not working in the first three months, you tear up the deal and both parties walk away and de-risk the entire thing, and again, drives incentives in the right way where the advisor is 100% incentivized at as much value as fast as possible. And so that's another thing that I tend to do and I've done it for a long time.
turns.zh: 我也是三个月悬崖的忠实粉丝。我所做的一件事，实际上我一直在做，就是倾听，在前三个月里，你会知道双方是否有效。你想要降低双方的风险，因为它确实应该被视为顾问和创始人之间的合作伙伴关系。如果创始人认为你在最初几个月没有增加价值，我认为他们应该撕毁它，双方继续前进。继续交易对创始人来说不好，坦率地说对顾问来说也不好，因为出于某种原因，他们无法在这种环境下增加价值。所以我喜欢一开始的三个月悬崖，如果在前三个月不起作用，你就撕毁协议，双方走开并降低整个事情的风险，然后再次以正确的方式推动激励，让顾问以尽可能快的价值获得 100% 的激励。这是我倾向于做的另一件事，而且我已经做了很长时间了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good tip. Basically don't do it for a year if you're vesting for advisors, probably not even to a year, but yeah.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常好的提示。如果你要为顾问授予权益，基本上一年内都不会这样做，甚至可能不会一年，但是是的。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: There's a bunch of ways to do it. Honestly, it's hard enough to find growth advisors that have capacity, so you got to also say like, "What can you do that the advisor's comfortable with?" But yeah, I mean just to be candid, I think you want to structure in a way where you're not dependent on the advisor over time. They're adding a ton of value, they're helping teach the team, they're probably bouncing around because your company's changing, your team's changing, your leaders are changing. But over time, and that can be years, but it shouldn't be indefinite. You shouldn't need an advisor forever.
turns.zh: 有很多方法可以做到这一点。老实说，找到有能力的增长顾问已经够难了，所以你还必须说，“你能做什么让顾问感到满意？”但是，是的，我的意思是坦白地说，我认为你希望以一种不随着时间的推移依赖于顾问的方式进行构建。他们增加了大量的价值，他们帮助教导团队，他们可能会因为你的公司在变化，你的团队在变化，你的领导者在变化而四处走动。但随着时间的推移，可能是几年，但不应该是无限期的。你不应该永远需要顾问。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I've seen a scenario where there's desire to keep the advisor on almost as insurance, like, "If something goes wrong, I just wanted to be able to pick up the phone." That can make sense. But I do think a good growth advisor is incentivized to share as much as possible, as fast as possible to have impact to train your team. And then whether you want to keep them on or not long term as an insurance policy or just to answer questions as things change, that should be a choice and not because, "If we lose the advisor. We're completely screwed." That would be a bad place for you to be in as a founder.
turns.zh: 我见过这样一种情况，人们希望让顾问继续工作，就像保险一样，比如“如果出现问题，我只想能够拿起电话。”这是有道理的。但我确实认为优秀的成长顾问会被激励尽可能多、尽可能快地分享，以便对培训你的团队产生影响。然后，无论你想将它们作为保险单长期保留还是不长期保留，或者只是在情况发生变化时回答问题，这都应该是一个选择，而不是因为“如果我们失去了顾问。我们就彻底完蛋了。”作为创始人，这对你来说是一个糟糕的处境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said it's hard to find a good advisor, 100% agree. Any advice for people to help them find an advisor that might be the right fit?
turns.zh: 你说很难找到一个好的顾问，100%同意。有什么建议可以帮助人们找到合适的顾问吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I would say there's more of them these days than there were even just five years ago or 10 years ago. Depending on your situation, if you're a founder, I would start with your investors. I think VCs have an amazing network of advisors. I get, I don't know, a couple requests a week that I'm not taking right now. But that from my experience and what I've seen, that's probably especially the high end VCs, the very talented VCs will have this network. And frankly, it's a great partnership as an advisor for you to have. You can help the companies, you can help the VCs and it helps you. So everybody wins, just asking other founders that had good experience, much like hiring.
turns.zh: 是的，我想说现在的数量比五年前或十年前还要多。根据你的情况，如果你是创始人，我会从你的投资者开始。我认为风险投资家拥有一个令人惊叹的顾问网络。我不知道，我每周都会收到一些请求，但我现在没有接受。但根据我的经验和我所看到的，这可能尤其是高端风险投资，非常有才华的风险投资将拥有这个网络。坦率地说，作为顾问，这是一个很好的合作伙伴关系。你可以帮助公司，你可以帮助风投，它也会帮助你。所以每个人都会赢，只需询问其他有良好经验的创始人，就像招聘一样。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: The third advice I would give is to find companies that are world-class at what you're trying to grow, what channel or skill you're looking at, and then reach out and see if there's a way to help that way. That's actually how I got started. I was at Tripadvisor and a prominent VC reached out. One of the companies they were working with needed some help on SEO. I was still in Canada at the time, got connected with them, had a phone call, had a significant impact through that one phone call. And rather than joining as an advisor, I essentially helped them out pro bono in exchange for, "Hey, I want to get connected in the Valley." So I was in Canada, I wanted to start another company, I wanted to get connected. So through that tactic where they reached out to a company that was known to be world-class at SEO, I think that was really smart on this VC's part.
turns.zh: 我给出的第三个建议是，找到在你想要发展的领域、你正在寻找的渠道或技能方面处于世界一流的公司，然后伸出援手，看看是否有办法提供帮助。我实际上就是这样开始的。我在 Tripadvisor 工作时，一位著名的风险投资家向我伸出了援手。他们合作的一家公司需要 SEO 方面的帮助。当时我还在加拿大，与他们取得了联系，打了一个电话，通过那一个电话产生了重大影响。我并没有以顾问的身份加入，而是无偿地帮助他们，以换取“嘿，我想在硅谷建立联系”。所以我在加拿大，我想创办另一家公司，我想建立联系。因此，通过他们接触到一家在 SEO 方面世界一流的公司的策略，我认为这对风险投资来说非常明智。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: And then maybe some advice to up and coming growth advisors would be that first one, I didn't take a single shred of equity or money and just tried to have as much impact as possible and to help out this company as much as possible and then make sure that I was able to get connected to other people that I wanted to meet in the Bay Area. And then kind of things snowballed from there.
turns.zh: 然后，也许对即将到来的增长顾问的一些建议是，第一个，我没有拿走一丁点股权或金钱，只是试图产生尽可能大的影响，尽可能地帮助这家公司，然后确保我能够与我想在湾区认识的其他人建立联系。然后事情就从那里滚雪球般滚滚而来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I definitely want to chat about how to become a growth advisor because I think people listening here might be like, "Oh, that sounds pretty good. Someday maybe I'll become a growth advisor." But before we get to that, what are things that an advisor are best suited for versus finding someone full-time versus no one? What are the ideal kind of problem sets for an advisor versus say, full-time hire person?
turns.zh: 我绝对想谈谈如何成为一名成长顾问，因为我认为在这里听的人可能会说，“哦，这听起来不错。也许有一天我会成为一名成长顾问。”但在此之前，我们先来了解一下，与寻找全职顾问和无人顾问相比，顾问最适合做哪些事情？对于顾问和全职雇员来说，理想的问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I would say your preference should always be to have somebody in-house. I'll start there because you want to have that as part of the culture. There's so much more that they can do when they're in-house. That being said, if you can't find somebody in-house, then bring on an advisor... Even if you bring on an advisor, some advice to founders would be you want to surround your team or at least one person that you've identified who's just a amazing world-class doer, even if they don't know growth, with a set of growth advisors so that they're learning, that's being put through the culture of the company and that knowledge stays inside of the company. So I'd say I would prefer to go internal, surround these people with great advisors and then take it from there. That would be how I approach it.
turns.zh: 我想说的是，您应该始终优先选择内部人员。我将从这里开始，因为你希望将其作为文化的一部分。当他们在公司内部时，他们可以做的事情还有很多。话虽这么说，如果你在内部找不到人，那就聘请一名顾问……即使你聘请了一名顾问，对创始人的一些建议是，你想要围绕你的团队或至少一个你认为是世界级的实干家的人，即使他们不了解增长，也要有一组增长顾问，以便他们不断学习，将其融入公司文化，并将知识保留在公司内部。所以我想说我更愿意进入内部，为这些人提供优秀的顾问，然后从那里开始。这就是我的处理方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So two thoughts here. One is I feel like this podcast is becoming an interesting way to discover awesome growth advisors. I think over time I'm building this directory of who are awesome, smart growth people that are open to advising. So that could be an interesting opportunity to just look through the folks on this podcast and-
turns.zh: 好的。所以这里有两个想法。一是我觉得这个播客正在成为发现优秀成长顾问的一种有趣方式。我想，随着时间的推移，我正在建立这个目录，列出谁是优秀的、聪明的、乐于提供建议的成长型人士。因此，这可能是一个有趣的机会，可以浏览一下这个播客中的人们，然后-

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yep, there's some great people that have been on here. Definitely.
turns.zh: 是的，这里有一些很棒的人。确实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Totally working my way through all the amazing least smart growth people and product leaders. The other is I've noticed they're a lot of the best growth advisors have worked with the same sorts of companies. I find Miro comes up a lot, Canva comes up a lot, Pinterest. All these people that have worked with say Pinterest that I hear about are just awesome. Casey comes to mind, Melissa Tan who's coming out with a podcast, I think she worked with them. Dropbox. Anyway, so maybe one idea, see who these companies work with as advisors and that can maybe point you to people that are worth exploring.
turns.zh: 我完全通过所有令人惊叹的最不聪明的增长人员和产品领导者来工作。另一个是我注意到他们中有很多最好的成长顾问都曾与同类公司合作过。我发现 Miro 出现了很多，Canva 出现了很多，Pinterest。所有与我合作过的人都说我听说过的 Pinterest 非常棒。我想到了凯西，梅丽莎·谭，她正在推出一个播客，我想她和他们一起工作过。 Dropbox。不管怎样，也许有一个想法，看看这些公司与谁合作作为顾问，这也许可以给你指出值得探索的人。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I mean, that's a good idea. It kind of goes back to something I mentioned earlier, which is companies that have a lot of traffic and that have a lot of users are a great learning ground for growth people and for advisors, because no matter how smart you are, you need the reps. You got to go to the growth gym and put in the reps, which is experiments. You've got to try things, things that are going to work, things that aren't going to work. There's a discipline of when something doesn't work, you can learn almost as much as when something works. But you need that traffic, you need that environment. And that's why certain companies have these great people coming out like Casey at Pinterest and other people that have been at these companies that have the traffic, have the culture to support it, to support growth. I don't think that's a coincidence why some of these companies have some great people coming from them.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这是个好主意。这有点回到我之前提到的，拥有大量流量和用户的公司对于成长型人才和顾问来说是一个很好的学习场所，因为无论你有多聪明，你都需要销售代表。你必须去健身房进行训练，这就是实验。你必须尝试一些事情，那些行得通的事情，那些行不通的事情。有一条原则是，当某件事不起作用时，你可以学到的东西几乎和某事起作用时一样多。但你需要那种流量，你需要那种环境。这就是为什么某些公司拥有像 Pinterest 的凯西这样的优秀人才，以及其他在这些公司工作过的人，他们拥有流量，拥有支持流量、支持增长的文化。我认为，其中一些公司拥有一些优秀人才，这并非巧合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other tip I just thought about as you were talking is everyone's launching a Substack newsletter that is doing any sort of advising because there's a lot of power in building an audience and creating kind of awareness of what you do. So I wonder if another tip is search Substack's directory of newsletters for specific things you're dealing with, like say, go to PLG or sales and you might find someone there."
turns.zh: 当你谈论的时候我刚刚想到的另一个建议是每个人都在推出一个 Substack 时事通讯，它正在提供任何形式的建议，因为在建立受众和提高人们对你所做的事情的认识方面有很大的力量。所以我想知道是否还有另一个技巧是搜索 Substack 的时事通讯目录以查找您正在处理的特定事务，例如，去 PLG 或销售部门，您可能会在那里找到人。”

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I haven't done that, but that seems like a reasonable way to do it.
turns.zh: 我还没有这样做，但这似乎是一个合理的方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's where we're all heading.
turns.zh: 这就是我们所有人的前进方向。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I'm not saying that the people on Substack have this. But as advice to the people listening, is when you're vetting for a growth advisor or growth talent, don't just wait it on the public halo of somebody. That's a common mistake I've seen where maybe somebody's done presentations at a conference or somebody's done... I don't know, but their Twitter following is broad. They can be excellent. That's not a disqualifier immediately, but just make sure not to make the hire just exclusively on that. I've made that mistake a few times and it's a common one to get into. So make sure you're vetting properly, even if somebody with a large following on Substack or Twitter. That's I think an important thing to keep in mind.
turns.zh: 我并不是说 Substack 上的人有这个。但给听众的建议是，当你审查成长顾问或成长人才时，不要只是等待某人的公众光环。这是我见过的一个常见错误，也许有人在会议上做过演示，或者有人做过……我不知道，但他们的 Twitter 关注者很广泛。他们可以很优秀。这并不是立即取消资格，但要确保不要仅仅以此为由进行聘用。我已经犯过几次这样的错误，而且这是一个很常见的错误。因此，即使某人在 Substack 或 Twitter 上拥有大量关注者，也要确保您进行了适当的审查。我认为这是一件需要牢记的重要事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 1000% agree. I always say that the best product leader is the best growth. People don't have time to sit on Twitter and tweet and write newsletters. They're doing the job, working, building, growing, and maybe eventually they get out of that and start writing. But I 1000% agree, there's a lot of people-
turns.zh: 1000%同意。我总是说，最好的产品领导者就是最好的成长。人们没有时间坐在推特上发推文和撰写时事通讯。他们正在做这份工作，工作、建设、成长，也许最终他们会摆脱这些并开始写作。但我1000%同意，有很多人-

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Well, not to disqualify all the people on Twitter.
turns.zh: 好吧，并不是要取消 Twitter 上所有人的资格。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对地。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Some of them are tweeting [inaudible 00:37:45], but my point is just don't over pivot on the halo. Just look at their past performance. What teams have they been on? What environment do they have? Do they really know growth? And sometimes they do, but I think it's a common mistake to say, "Oh yeah, they have a large following, let's hire this person." That's poorly.
turns.zh: 他们中的一些人正在发推文 [听不清 00:37:45]，但我的观点是不要过度关注光环。看看他们过去的表现就知道了。他们曾效力过哪些球队？他们有什么环境？他们真的懂得成长吗？有时他们会这样做，但我认为说“哦，是的，他们有很多追随者，让我们雇用这个人”是一个常见的错误。那就不好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 1000% agree. Rarely does a celebrity hire that seems really genius on Twitter and Substack end up being as amazing as you think.
turns.zh: 1000%同意。在 Twitter 和 Substack 上看似真正天才的名人聘用，很少会像你想象的那样令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, it does happen, but yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，它确实发生了，但是是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It does happen. Absolutely. One last question around this topic. People listening might want to become growth advisors, I'd mentioned this earlier. Is there any other advice you want to share? Just like, "If you want to become a growth advisor someday, here's what you should think about."
turns.zh: 它确实发生了。绝对地。围绕这个主题的最后一个问题。我之前提到过，倾听的人可能想成为成长顾问。您还有其他建议要分享吗？就像，“如果你有一天想成为一名成长顾问，这就是你应该考虑的事情。”

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I think the right mental model as a growth advisor is around the same one as an investor. So the most important thing an advisor can do aside from having impact and knowing their craft is picking which companies to work with, especially if you're working for equity. So I'll only speak to that, but you're basically putting in your time, you're picking likely a smaller number. You only have so many hours in the day of companies to work with and you want to make sure there's a likely exit in the future. So for me personally, I have a spreadsheet, like most big decisions that I make in my life. Over the years I've just added criteria and questions to ask myself about the company and then reflect on, "Okay, is this kind of checking all the boxes for a likely outcome?" Because you don't just need to be successful, you need to be successful and for the company to be successful and for there to be liquidity of that.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为作为一名成长顾问的正确思维模式与作为一名投资者大致相同。因此，除了发挥影响力和了解自己的技能之外，顾问可以做的最重要的事情就是选择与哪些公司合作，特别是如果您正在为股权工作。所以我只会谈论这一点，但你基本上投入了时间，你可能会选择一个较小的数字。你每天只有这么多时间可以与公司合作，并且你想确保未来有可能退出。因此，就我个人而言，我有一个电子表格，就像我一生中做出的大多数重大决定一样。多年来，我只是添加了一些标准和问题来询问自己关于公司的情况，然后反思，“好吧，这是一种检查所有方框以获得可能结果的方式吗？”因为你不仅需要成功，你还需要成功，公司也需要成功，公司需要有流动性。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So you need to put yourself in the shoes of an investor and look at it as an investment. That is arguably the most important thing because you can go and do a great job and then wait many years and potentially not see any reward for it. And I think that's the nice thing about the equity structure in that you're tied in the same incentives with the founder, which is just great in terms of any relationship to have the same incentives, but you want to make sure that there's a good likelihood of a decent outcome down the road.
turns.zh: 因此，您需要将自己置于投资者的立场上，并将其视为一项投资。这可以说是最重要的事情，因为你可以去做一份出色的工作，然后等待很多年，但可能看不到任何回报。我认为股权结构的好处在于，你与创始人有着相同的激励措施，这对于拥有相同激励措施的任何关系来说都是很好的，但你要确保未来很有可能取得不错的结果。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: If I can throw another one in.
turns.zh: 如果我能再扔一个进去就好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对是。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: The other piece of advice I would give is it can take a long time for some of these companies to be successful. That's okay. You should expect that. In fact, you should just go in with that mindset. When I'm deciding to work with a company, I'm in there for 10 years and I know that and I say that. And I say, "I'm in. We're in this together if I choose to work with the company." But it does mean that the structure of the deal needs to reflect that. So you need to have a long tail at the end.
turns.zh: 我要给出的另一条建议是，其中一些公司可能需要很长时间才能取得成功。没关系。你应该预料到这一点。事实上，你应该抱着这样的心态去做。当我决定与一家公司合作时，我已经在那里工作了 10 年，我知道这一点，我也这么说。我说：“我同意。如果我选​​择与公司合作，我们就会一起参与。”但这确实意味着交易结构需要反映这一点。所以你最后需要有一条长尾巴。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So if you're taking options or RSUs and it's pure of the equity, make sure you have the time for that to happen. There would be nothing worse than putting your heart and soul having impact and then waiting, I don't know, a couple years and then your equity expires. So you make sure there's a long tail. I mean, it can literally take over 10 years for these companies to exit. And you should be okay with that. I think that's okay. You're taking some risks. They're taking some risk on you and that's a great partnership, but you'll just need the time for that. So advice to growth advisors, make sure to ask for a long tail so that you don't end up in a bad spot in the end. And that incentives, again, are perfectly aligned between the founder and the advisor.
turns.zh: 因此，如果您购买期权或 RSU，并且纯粹是股权，请确保您有时间这样做。没有什么比全心全意地发挥影响力然后等待，我不知道，几年之后你的股权到期更糟糕的了。所以你要确保有一条长尾巴。我的意思是，这些公司实际上可能需要 10 多年才能退出。你应该对此感到满意。我认为没关系。你正在冒一些风险。他们让你承担一些风险，这是一个很好的合作伙伴关系，但你只需要时间。因此，给增长顾问的建议是，一定要要求长尾，这样你最终就不会陷入困境。而且，创始人和顾问之间的激励措施是完全一致的。
