turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I want to segue to a different topic, SEO. You're kind of the... You tell me, but it feels like you're one of the earliest SEO people in tech. You helped grow Tripadvisor many years ago and it was mostly SEO-driven. I think you innovated a lot of SEO tactics and strategies. And then you helped Pinterest, Thumbtack, other companies that are very SEO-driven. You talked about how many companies grow through one channel and these are all very SEO-driven companies. I imagine Shopify has a lot of SEO work that's happening right now with you there. And so I want to chat about SEO. So I guess broadly SEO is like... It's like this amazing growth channel. It's basically free. It continues to work after you stop doing any work on it for a while. Many founders think about, "Should we invest in SEO? How do we approach SEO?" So maybe just as a first question, what are signs that your product and company is a good fit for SEO being potentially a huge channel for growth?
turns.zh: 所以我想转向另一个主题，SEO。你是那种......你告诉我，但感觉你是技术领域最早的 SEO 人员之一。许多年前，您帮助 Tripadvisor 发展，而且主要是 SEO 驱动的。我认为你创新了很多 SEO 策略和策略。然后你帮助了 Pinterest、Thumbtack 以及其他非常注重 SEO 的公司。您谈到有多少公司通过一种渠道实现增长，这些公司都是 SEO 驱动的公司。我想 Shopify 现在有很多 SEO 工作正在与您一起进行。所以我想谈谈 SEO。所以我想广义上 SEO 就像......就像这个惊人的增长渠道。基本上是免费的。当您停止对其进行任何操作一段时间后，它仍会继续工作。许多创始人都会思考，“我们应该投资SEO吗？我们如何进行SEO？”因此，也许作为第一个问题，有哪些迹象表明您的产品和公司非常适合 SEO，成为潜在的巨大增长渠道？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I've been doing SEO for a really long time. It's a lot of fun and certainly being a supervisor was a great learning ground for that, that we were able to really innovate and try new things there. In terms of the playbook that we built out. That was a lot of fun, those years.
turns.zh: 是的，我做SEO已经很长时间了。这很有趣，当然，成为一名主管是一个很好的学习基础，我们能够在那里真正创新并尝试新事物。就我们制定的剧本而言。那些年，真是太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Couple thoughts. The first one would be I do think there's an SEO play in any company. Maybe at a different extent, but Google is such a large funnel of existing demand for your product or your product area that there's usually an angle to get some SEO traffic there. So I do think it applies to most companies. I would say if you're an early product that the world's never seen, it's a brand new thing, there might be some creation, some demand creation you need to do, but most of the time there's existing demand in Google where you can harvest demand or there's queries that are related to your topic that you can start ranking for to start building brand awareness. So there's always some angle.
turns.zh: 夫妻的想法。第一个是我确实认为任何公司都存在搜索引擎优化。也许程度不同，但谷歌是你的产品或产品领域现有需求的一个大漏斗，通常有一个角度可以在那里获得一些搜索引擎优化流量。所以我确实认为这适用于大多数公司。我想说，如果你是一个世界上从未见过的早期产品，它是一个全新的东西，你可能需要做一些创造，一些需求创造，但大多数时候谷歌中有现有的需求，你可以收获需求，或者有与你的主题相关的查询，你可以开始排名以开始建立品牌知名度。所以总有一些角度。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: And then I kind of divide websites or online products into two categories. There's the ones which are smaller sites, small number of pages, very targeted at your product and don't have this kind of loop of creating new pages automatically. Most eCommerce sites actually have would a number of pages around the products and about us, those types of pages. That's one type of sites. Let's say they have dozen pages. And then there's other ones with thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, millions of pages which are either user generated content like Tripadvisor and Pinterest and others, or marketplaces like Thumbtack and other types of websites like that. Those are generally easier to see a huge amount of impact very quickly because there's such a large optimization surface and ideally it's growing and generating traffic automatically.
turns.zh: 然后我将网站或在线产品分为两类。有些网站较小，页面数量较少，非常针对您的产品，并且没有这种自动创建新页面的循环。大多数电子商务网站实际上都有许多关于产品和关于我们的页面，这些类型的页面。这是网站的一种类型。假设它们有十几页。还有其他拥有数千、数万、数十万、数百万页面的页面，这些页面要么是用户生成的内容，如 Tripadvisor 和 Pinterest 等，要么是市场，如 Thumbtack 和其他类型的网站。这些通常更容易很快地看到巨大的影响，因为有如此大的优化表面，并且理想情况下它会自动增长并产生流量。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I've always thought of LinkedIn as just such a great example of this where you have this viral loop where if you recall when it was just starting, everybody was getting these invites from LinkedIn. Those come and go. You get an invite, you register, you don't. That happens. But the byproduct is when people join, they create this beautiful lightning page, which is your profile that gets indexed. It's kind of like a viral loop feeding an SEO loop that continues to grow. So that's a good example of use generated content which kind of feeds on itself and grows. So there's those two categories. Going back to the first category, if you only have a small handful of pages, the way to think about that is you certainly want to optimize those pages, then you want to start creating content that speaks to your audience beyond that. So you need a content strategy, whether it's a blog or creating new parts of your site that address questions that your audience might have. But generally speaking, I think there's an SEO play in any company and there's just different tactics, strategies, and approaches to get there.
turns.zh: 我一直认为 LinkedIn 就是一个很好的例子，你会发现这种病毒式循环，如果你还记得它刚开始的时候，每个人都会收到来自 LinkedIn 的邀请。那些来来去去。你收到邀请，你注册，但你没有。就会发生这种情况。但副产品是当人们加入时，他们创建了这个美丽的闪电页面，这是您的个人资料被索引的地方。这有点像一个病毒循环，为一个持续增长的 SEO 循环提供动力。这是使用生成内容的一个很好的例子，它可以自我滋养并增长。所以有这两类。回到第一类，如果您只有一小部分页面，那么考虑这一点的方法是您当然想要优化这些页面，然后您想要开始创建与您的受众对话的内容。因此，您需要一个内容策略，无论是博客还是创建网站的新部分来解决受众可能提出的问题。但总的来说，我认为任何公司都存在 SEO 策略，只是有不同的策略、策略和方法来实现这一目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I never thought of it that way, that there's kind of these two buckets. So the first bucket is like you don't have a ton of pages that naturally are generated as a part of your experience. And the second is you do. I guess in the second bucket I think of Reddit and Glassdoor and Quora, Tripadvisor, a great example, Pinterest. In the first bucket is the way to generate pages. Basically, it's editorially write content and have people write things for you. Is that generally the strategy?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我从来没有这样想过，有这样两个桶。因此，第一个桶就像您没有大量作为您的体验的一部分自然生成的页面。第二个是你做的。我想在第二个桶中，我会想到 Reddit、Glassdoor 和 Quora、Tripadvisor、Pinterest 就是一个很好的例子。第一个桶是生成页面的方式。基本上，它是编辑性地编写内容并让人们为您编写内容。这通常是策略吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: There's different ways of doing it, but a good content strategy is a kind of tried and true approach. Definitely.
turns.zh: 有不同的方法可以做到这一点，但良好的内容策略是一种经过考验的真实方法。确实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And in that bucket of you don't naturally have a ton of pages, can you primarily grow through SEO? Or is SEO always going to be this minority channel and you have to find something else?
turns.zh: 对于这样的人来说，你自然不会有大量的页面，你能主要通过搜索引擎优化来成长吗？或者 SEO 总是会成为少数渠道，而你必须寻找其他东西？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: No, it can be a big channel. This is also about creating content, but it's not your users creating the content. You have to go create the content and have some high quality answer to a question that's being asked on Google. I think one thing to keep in mind with SEO is entire industries are based off of single keywords. I remember when I was in the travel industry that literally companies were bought and sold based on one keyword rank. So it's not like, "Oh, it's a little bit of traffic." And I think this is a bit unintuitive with growth. A lot of people, they'll think of growth as linear or it's another channel, it's another thing. I mean, growth done right is exponential. It literally is company changing.
turns.zh: 不，它可以是一个大通道。这也是关于创建内容，但不是您的用户创建内容。你必须去创建内容，并对 Google 上提出的问题提供高质量的答案。我认为关于 SEO 需要记住的一件事是整个行业都是基于单个关键词的。我记得当我从事旅游业时，公司实际上是根据一个关键词排名进行买卖的。所以这并不是“哦，有点流量”。我认为这对于增长来说有点不直观。很多人会认为增长是线性的，或者是另一个渠道，这是另一回事。我的意思是，正确的增长是指数级的。这实际上是公司的变革。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: When you're talking specifically about SEO, keep in mind the world is searching for that thing, targeted on that one keyword and likely you're clicking the number one search result. So getting that number one spot is not like, "Oh, that's a little bit of traffic." You can literally build an entire business around that first spot. So don't think that's... Well, maybe it is commonly known, I'm not sure, but it's definitely something that is non-obvious or intuitive I think to most people. And if you have an entire SEO team working on one keyword, I don't think that's crazy because a small number of keywords can define an entire industry or a business.
turns.zh: 当您专门谈论搜索引擎优化时，请记住，全世界都在搜索该东西，针对该关键字，并且您可能正在点击排名第一的搜索结果。因此，获得第一名并不像“哦，这只是一点点流量。”您实际上可以围绕第一个位置建立整个业务。所以不要认为这是……好吧，也许这是众所周知的，我不确定，但我认为对大多数人来说这绝对是非显而易见或直观的东西。如果你有一个完整的 SEO 团队致力于一个关键字，我认为这并不疯狂，因为少量的关键字可以定义整个行业或企业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that sort of situation when keyword's building a massive company?
turns.zh: 当关键字建立一家大型公司时，有这种情况的例子吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I mean there's a lot I'm sure. I can speak to my own company that I sold to Tripadvisor. It was called TravelPod. It was a travel blogging website where you can think WordPress, but for travel, which I started earlier. It was the first site to do that. I made the mistake of not knowing SEO or growth before I sold the company. And so that was a great learning for me. When I went in, this is a story where we're looking to acquire another site and I thought the product was pretty poor. I remember talking to the founder and thinking... He'd asked me if we'd want to acquire it, and, "The product's terrible. Why would I want to acquire that?" He's like, "Yeah, they're 10 times bigger than you." And, "What?" That was when I realized, "Okay, we've been building a great product and great engineering culture and it is important, but you really need to know this growth stuff." So that's actually the moment I shifted to, "All right, we have to really know these growth levers."
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是我确信很多事情。我可以谈谈我自己卖给 Tripadvisor 的公司。它被称为 TravelPod。这是一个旅行博客网站，你可以在其中想到 WordPress，但针对旅行，我之前就开始了。这是第一个这样做的网站。在出售公司之前，我犯了一个不了解搜索引擎优化或增长的错误。所以这对我来说是一个很好的学习。当我进去时，这是一个我们正在寻求收购另一个网站的故事，我认为该产品非常糟糕。我记得与创始人交谈并思考......他问我是否想收购它，并且，“这个产品很糟糕。我为什么要收购它？”他说：“是的，它们比你大 10 倍。”然后，“什么？”就在那时我意识到，“好吧，我们一直在打造出色的产品和出色的工程文化，这很重要，但你确实需要了解这些增长的东西。”所以这实际上是我转向“好吧，我们必须真正了解这些增长杠杆”的时刻。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: In that space, the number one keyword was Travel Blog. And so owning that was a big deal and we did not own it. I think we ranked number two for a really long time. I can't remember if we got it in the end, but that's just one example where... And there was many, many travel businesses where I always loved looking at a business and trying to figure out, "What's their growth loop? How did they do that?" And it's not like, "Oh, it's a great business. It just grew." Most of the time it's price line crushed it at SEM. Facebook crushed it at a viral loop where you got tagged in a photo, you got an email and you had to go register because there's a photo of you somewhere you really want to see. Tripadvisor did a great job at SEO. In [inaudible 00:49:14], it's just one really strong channel that propelled the company forward. And in this case, it can literally come down to one keyword like we had at TravelPod.
turns.zh: 在这个领域，排名第一的关键词是旅游博客。因此，拥有它是一件大事，但我们并不拥有它。我认为我们在很长一段时间内排名第二。我不记得我们最终是否得到了它，但这只是一个例子......而且有很多很多旅游企业，我总是喜欢观察一家企业并试图弄清楚，“他们的增长循环是什么？他们是如何做到的？”这并不是说，“哦，这是一项伟大的业务。它刚刚成长起来。”大多数时候，它的价格线在 SEM 上被压垮了。 Facebook 以病毒式循环的方式摧毁了它，你在照片中被标记，你收到一封电子邮件，你必须去注册，因为在你真正想看的地方有一张你的照片。 Tripadvisor 在 SEO 方面做得非常出色。在 [听不清 00:49:14] 中，这只是推动公司前进的一个非常强大的渠道。在这种情况下，它实际上可以归结为一个关键字，就像我们在 TravelPod 中所做的那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So maybe it's a good time just to give a people a mental model of the different channels/loops that exist. So you've talked about SEO is one, paid search is one. What's the collection for people to think about? Usually as you said, one of the use is the primary source of growth for a company.
turns.zh: 因此，也许现在是为人们提供现有不同渠道/循环的心智模型的好时机。所以你谈到了 SEO 是其中之一，付费搜索是其中之一。值得人们思考的收藏是什么？通常正如您所说，其中一项用途是公司增长的主要来源。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, there's a variety of them. I think you have to look at where the intent is right now. It does change over time, but you have social channels like TikTok, Instagram. Influencers are a great area to engage with there. You have SEO, you have search. I think ChatGPT is another upcoming one that we might want to talk about a little bit where I do think we've never seen that kind of growth for search before and that's a platform that we have to start thinking about how do we optimize for it. Google just announced there are recent changes. They're going to be putting in an AI box at the top, the searchers also, how do you optimize in a world where it's not so much about optimizing for the platform, but teaching the AI what you do and why you're the best in the world at it. So that's another whole area that we could talk about, but that's a big channel I think that that's growing.
turns.zh: 是的，有各种各样的。我认为你现在必须看看意图在哪里。它确实会随着时间的推移而改变，但你有 TikTok、Instagram 等社交渠道。有影响力的人是一个很好的接触领域。你有搜索引擎优化，你有搜索。我认为 ChatGPT 是另一个即将推出的平台，我们可能想稍微讨论一下，我认为我们以前从未见过搜索的这种增长，这是一个我们必须开始思考如何优化它的平台。谷歌刚刚宣布最近有一些变化。他们将在顶部放置一个人工智能框，搜索者也是如此，在这个世界中，你如何优化，而不是针对平台进行优化，而是教人工智能你做什么以及为什么你是世界上最好的。这是我们可以讨论的另一个整体领域，但我认为这是一个正在增长的大渠道。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Viral loops are always a powerful thing if you can get them to work. That's more about psychology and channel optimization, where you want people to be incentivized to share the product that you have with their friends and then to have their friends come back and register. So you can have one viral loop, you can have secondary viral loops, you can bolt viral loops on your existing products. There's different ways of doing this. And then just backing up. When I think about growth, I don't think about a specific... It's not growth equals SEO and Instagram. For me, growth equals whatever it takes to move the needle. So I get this question all the time, "How do you build a growth team? What does a growth team do?" And I say whatever it takes. That could be zero to one building a new product. It could be M&A, it could be SEO, it could be social, it could be onboarding.
turns.zh: 如果你能让病毒式循环发挥作用，它总是一个强大的东西。这更多的是关于心理学和渠道优化，您希望人们受到激励与他们的朋友分享您拥有的产品，然后让他们的朋友回来注册。因此，您可以拥有一个病毒循环，也可以拥有二级病毒循环，还可以将病毒循环固定在现有产品上。有不同的方法可以做到这一点。然后只需备份即可。当我考虑增长时，我不会考虑具体的……增长并不等于 SEO 和 Instagram。对我来说，增长就等于不惜一切代价推动发展。所以我总是收到这样的问题：“如何建立增长团队？增长团队做什么？”我会说无论需要什么。开发新产品可能是零到一。可能是并购，可能是搜索引擎优化，可能是社交，也可能是入职。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I think that's a better framework to look at. And then if you look at it through that lens, then partnerships easily folds into that where I've seen a lot of businesses get very big on just really clever partnerships, either strategic or broad kind of affiliate based partnerships. So there's a lot of channels. I definitely wouldn't restrict the scope of a growth team to just a small subset, but have a very wide funnel or at least strategy in terms of just test a lot of different things and go after the channels that work and pivot when it does, and then really lean into the one or two or three that really work because sometimes that's all it takes for business.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个更好的框架。然后，如果你从这个角度来看，那么合作伙伴关系很容易就会变成这样，我看到很多企业通过真正聪明的合作伙伴关系变得非常大，无论是战略合作伙伴关系还是广泛的基于联盟的合作伙伴关系。所以渠道很多。我绝对不会将增长团队的范围限制在一小部分，而是拥有一个非常广泛的漏斗或至少是测试许多不同事物的策略，并追求有效的渠道并在有效时进行调整，然后真正倾向于真正有效的一两个或三个，因为有时这就是业务所需要的全部。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, you definitely nerd sniped me with the ChatGPT, so let's just spend some time there. I think this relates to just the general sense that SEO is always changing and it feels like this is an SEM I guess in this case too. And ChatGPT and Bard, I guess, is maybe the latest change. So what should we know there?
turns.zh: 好吧，你绝对是个书呆子用 ChatGPT 狙击了我，所以我们就在那里花点时间吧。我认为这与 SEO 总是在变化的一般感觉有关，我想在这种情况下，感觉就像是 SEM。我想，ChatGPT 和 Bard 可能是最新的变化。那么我们应该知道什么呢？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, I think we're all still trying to figure it out. I was at Google IO last week or the week before. As soon as I saw the search result with the big box of AI, answers at the top, having done this for so long, I immediately knew the impact that I think is about to come. I've seen this play out in travel where Google acquired ITA and did flight search and hotel search. Generally, it's great for users and great for Google and the search engines, but makes it a little bit difficult for the publishers and the sites that are adding value to the ecosystem through being ranked in search results.
turns.zh: 是的，我想我们都还在努力弄清楚。上周或前一周我参加了 Google IO。当我看到搜索结果，上面有人工智能的大盒子，答案在顶部，做了这么久，我立即知道我认为即将到来的影响。我在旅游业中看到了这种情况，谷歌收购了 ITA，并进行了航班搜索和酒店搜索。一般来说，这对用户、谷歌和搜索引擎来说都很好，但对于出版商和通过在搜索结果中排名为生态系统增加价值的网站来说有点困难。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So what we're about to see is basically Google, what they showed was a big box on top of the search results that answers the query directly. So if you think about that, that means that there's a lot of queries right now that users are clicking through down on the organic links and getting their answer there, which will be answered directly in the search result. We've seen this play out over the last five to 10 years where more and more answers are being shown at the top. Every time something changes, entire industries are disrupted or are changed. And I think that's going to happen again.
turns.zh: 所以我们将看到的基本上是谷歌，他们展示的是搜索结果顶部的一个大框，可以直接回答查询。因此，如果您考虑一下，这意味着现在有很多查询，用户点击有机链接并在那里获得答案，这些答案将直接在搜索结果中得到解答。在过去的五到十年里，我们已经看到了这种情况的发生，越来越多的答案显示在顶部。每当有事情发生变化时，整个行业就会被扰乱或改变。我认为这种情况还会再次发生。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So there's different types of keywords. There's transactional ones like e-commerce keywords with purchase intent. There's navigational ones where you're trying to get somewhere. And there's informational keywords, which is, "I have a question. I'm looking for an answer." It's pretty broad. It's a big area. I think that last category of keywords is particularly at risk. So if anybody listening to this is currently getting traffic on those, you should start thinking about what does that mean when things start changing. And I think the changes will be... We'll probably start seeing things shift to paid. You have to pay for that free traffic.
turns.zh: 所以有不同类型的关键词。有交易性的关键词，例如具有购买意图的电子商务关键词。有导航功能，您可以尝试到达某个地方。还有信息性关键字，即“我有一个问题。我正在寻找答案”。它相当广泛。这是一个很大的区域。我认为最后一类关键词尤其面临风险。因此，如果任何收听此内容的人目前正在获得这些流量，您应该开始思考当事情开始发生变化时这意味着什么。我认为变化将是......我们可能会开始看到事情转向付费。您必须为免费流量付费。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: The second one is there may just be a case where those keywords just don't get many clicks anymore. You might drop down to a very small number of clicks, if at all, because questions will get answered directly in the search results. So it's a big shift. We have to see how things land, but that's, I think over the next 12 to 24 months, if history repeats itself, we'll see that channel change. We've seen this play out in all the different channels. They kind of evolve generally. You can't blame the companies are doing what they have to do. ChatGPT is now 50% of my daily searches and not Google. So I think Google has to react and this is what we'll see. So from a growth perspective, definitely something to start to think about.
turns.zh: 第二个是可能存在这样的情况：这些关键字不再获得很多点击。如果有的话，您可能会减少点击次数，因为问题将直接在搜索结果中得到解答。所以这是一个很大的转变。我们必须看看事情如何发展，但我认为在接下来的 12 到 24 个月内，如果历史重演，我们将看到渠道发生变化。我们已经在所有不同的渠道中看到了这种情况的发生。它们总体上是进化的。你不能责怪这些公司正在做他们必须做的事情。现在，我日常搜索的 50% 都是 ChatGPT，而不是 Google。所以我认为谷歌必须做出反应，这就是我们将看到的。因此，从增长的角度来看，绝对是值得开始考虑的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super fascinating. I think about my newsletter and now Google suck it all up and just tell you all the answers. Great. Good news for me.
turns.zh: 超级迷人。我想到了我的时事通讯，现在谷歌把它全部吸收了，只是告诉你所有的答案。伟大的。对我来说是个好消息。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: [inaudible 00:54:34].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And change is great. Things don't-
turns.zh: 是的。是的。变化是巨大的。事情不-

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: It's exciting. It's exciting. I'm just geeking out on growth a little bit, we haven't had a big platform change in a long time. So I'm like, "All right, cool. Let's go see what we can do here. How do you optimize this? How do you get listed if you can?" We're not sure where the placements will be, but that will be the new game.
turns.zh: 这很令人兴奋。这很令人兴奋。我只是在关注增长，我们已经很长时间没有进行过大的平台改变了。所以我想，“好吧，酷。让我们看看我们能在这里做什么。你如何优化它？如果可以的话，你如何被列出？”我们不确定放置位置在哪里，但这将是新游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's actually a lennybot.com that is a GPT bot trained on my content that there's a newsletter post about how it was all built so you could build your own. And so I think my new goal is going to have to convince people to go to lennybot.com instead of Google. Wish me luck.
turns.zh: 是的，实际上有一个 lennybot.com，它是一个根据我的内容进行训练的 GPT 机器人，其中有一篇新闻通讯文章介绍了它的全部构建方式，以便您可以构建自己的机器人。因此，我认为我的新目标必须说服人们访问 lennybot.com 而不是 Google。祝我好运。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Hey, you got to lean into it. Yeah, we have a shop.ai, this great AI-based shopping engine. And I'll tell you, I bought so much on it. It's so good. The more you use these technologies, the more you realize how good they are. And that's something biggest coming. It's not just, "Oh yeah, there's another change." I was summarizing the Google change is to some people and originally was thinking this is the biggest change in the last 10 years. And then when I reflected on the last 10 years, I thought this is actually the biggest change since the inception of Google actually. I don't think we've seen something as profound as what's coming. And you really need to get ready for it.
turns.zh: 嘿，你必须靠进去。是的，我们有一个 shop.ai，这是一个很棒的基于人工智能的购物引擎。我会告诉你，我在上面买了很多东西。太好了。您使用这些技术的次数越多，您就越意识到它们的优点。这是最重要的事情即将到来。这不仅仅是“哦，是的，还有另一个变化”。我正在总结谷歌的变化对某些人来说，最初认为这是过去 10 年来最大的变化。然后当我回顾过去的十年时，我认为这实际上是谷歌成立以来最大的变化。我认为我们还没有看到像即将发生的事情那样深刻的事情。你真的需要为此做好准备。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've been using ChatGPT for helping me with interview questions actually, and once in a while there's like a really good one.
turns.zh: 是的，实际上我一直在使用 ChatGPT 来帮助我解决面试问题，偶尔会出现一个非常好的问题。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Oh, that's cool.
turns.zh: 哦，那太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So thank you ChatGPT, bringing me good things also. Maybe one more question along these lines around kind of connecting advisorship in SEO. Would you suggest when you're starting to think about SEO, starting to invest in SEO, you might be listening to this feeling like, "I got to think about SEO," does it make sense to bring on, say, SEO advisor like you? I know you're not available currently, but other folks like you or are an agency that is really good at this stuff or bring on someone full time? Do you have any kind of frameworks for thinking about which direction to go?
turns.zh: 所以谢谢ChatGPT，也给我带来了好东西。也许还有一个关于 SEO 中的连接咨询的问题。您是否会建议，当您开始考虑 SEO、开始投资 SEO 时，您可能会听到这样的感觉，“我必须考虑 SEO”，那么聘请像您这样的 SEO 顾问是否有意义？我知道您目前没空，但其他像您一样的人或者是一家真正擅长这件事的机构，或者聘请了全职人员？您有什么框架来思考要走哪个方向？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: It's hard for an agency or a pure advisor without internal help to do a really good job without internal talent at the center. So I would say I would start with just hire somebody internally and give them the mandate and incentivize them correctly to go and own this channel. Even if they don't know SEO, my advice would be get an engineer, get somebody who is just a relentless doer who wants to learn this and surround them with great advisors that I've just seen that work really well.
turns.zh: 对于没有内部帮助的机构或纯粹的顾问来说，如果没有内部人才作为中心，就很难真正做好工作。所以我想说，我会首先在内部雇用一个人，给他们授权，并正确地激励他们去拥有这个频道。即使他们不了解搜索引擎优化，我的建议也是找一位工程师，找一个想要学习这一点的不懈实干家，并让他们身边有优秀的顾问，我刚刚看到这些顾问工作得非常好。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: There are some good agencies out there. Agencies will be working with multiple companies, so it's a little bit harder to get the same impact from an agency. It can work sometimes. But my preference is generally a last resort would be an agency. And I'd much rather have somebody who's internal who knows the business, who knows the keywords, who can have the knowledge internally inside the company permanently and help grow a team around them and have succession in place and a proper team so that you're not too dependent on this one person. But that would be my go-to. And then if you're really stuck, you can use agencies, but my default would be having somebody internal supplemented with agencies if you have to. Sorry, SEO is very specific. I mean, it's a very tight channel that knowing certain things about it can have a big impact. I think you do want people that have that experience that can bring that in from the outside to augmenting internal teams. It'll take a really long time to learn it.
turns.zh: 那里有一些不错的机构。代理机构将与多家公司合作，因此从代理机构获得相同的影响有点困难。有时它可以起作用。但我的偏好通常是最后的手段是代理机构。我更希望有一个了解业务、了解关键词、能够永久掌握公司内部知识并帮助围绕他们发展团队的内部人士，并拥有适当的继任者和适当的团队，这样你就不会太依赖这个人。但这将是我的首选。然后，如果你真的陷入困境，你可以使用代理机构，但我的默认设置是在必要时让内部人员通过代理机构进行补充。抱歉，SEO 非常具体。我的意思是，这是一个非常紧密的渠道，了解它的某些事情可以产生很大的影响。我认为你确实需要拥有这种经验的人，可以将外部的经验引入到内部团队中。真的要花很长时间才能学会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I was going to ask that. So you ideally want to find someone that's done it before that isn't just a relentless learner, but is that plus, has done SEO in the past?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我正想问这个。因此，您理想情况下希望找到以前做过这件事的人，而不仅仅是一个不懈的学习者，而且是过去做过 SEO 的人吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Oh, yeah. Ideally, you hire an amazing SEO person who can bring internal. Second would be somebody amazing who can get things done, surround them with advisors. And then in my stack rank, the third would be agencies.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。理想情况下，您聘请一位出色的 SEO 人员，可以带来内部。其次是那些能够把事情做好的人，周围都是顾问。然后在我的堆栈排名中，第三位是代理机构。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And then the other kind of common issue with SEOs, it takes a long time to show impact. Do you have just a rule of thumb of just give them this much time to see if they can make an impact?
turns.zh: 惊人的。 SEO 的另一种常见问题是，需要很长时间才能显现出影响。您是否有一个经验法则，就是给他们这么多时间来看看他们是否能产生影响？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I'd say a few things. I'd say if you already have content and pages that are pretty good and getting a decent amount of traffic, it doesn't necessarily have to take a long time. So that would be my first reaction. It can take a long time. Generally, it takes a long time when you have to build new content. So the way to think about Google is it is going to take your content, it's going to show it to its users, people that are searching, and it's going to determine which piece of content is the best to ranked highly. It's not just about little tricks and links and keyword ratios. Those days are over. Those do matter, but it's not purely about that. And if you have a new piece of content, it takes time for Google to build enough trust to say, "Okay, I'm going to start showing this to users now" and then start collecting user feedback and then rank it appropriately. That can take some time.
turns.zh: 我想说几句话。我想说，如果您已经拥有相当不错的内容和页面并且获得了相当多的流量，那么不一定需要花费很长时间。这就是我的第一反应。这可能需要很长时间。一般来说，当你必须构建新内容时，需要很长时间。因此，考虑谷歌的方式是，它将获取你的内容，将其展示给用户，正在搜索的人，并将确定哪一段内容最适合排名靠前。这不仅仅是小技巧、链接和关键词比率。那些日子已经结束了。这些确实很重要，但不仅仅是这个。如果你有一个新的内容，谷歌需要时间来建立足够的信任，说：“好吧，我现在要开始向用户展示它”，然后开始收集用户反馈，然后对其进行适当的排名。这可能需要一些时间。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: But if you have existing pages that are ranking eight and they're already on the first page, it doesn't always happen. But I've certainly seen it, in fact more common than not that you could have sometimes hundreds of percentages of lift very quickly. And it depends what you're starting with, is probably the right way to think about it. So if I'm trying to summarize it, I would say 12 months is probably max. If you can't see impact in 12 months, there's something wrong. If you have existing content, it could happen pretty early. It could happen on day one. Actually I've seen that happen. If you have to build new parts of the site, it can take months. I've seen that happen in companies I've worked with where I think it would be like a quarter, we had to wait till we saw a big lift. So it's somewhere between three to 12 months.
turns.zh: 但是，如果您现有的页面排名第八并且它们已经位于首页上，则这种情况并不总是会发生。但我确实见过这种情况，事实上，更常见的是，有时您可以很快获得数百%的升力。这取决于你从什么开始，这可能是正确的思考方式。因此，如果我试图总结一下，我会说 12 个月可能是最长的。如果您在 12 个月内看不到效果，则说明有问题。如果您有现有内容，那么它可能会很早就发生。这可能会在第一天发生。事实上我已经看到这种情况发生了。如果您必须构建网站的新部分，可能需要几个月的时间。我在与我合作过的公司中看到过这种情况，我认为大约是一个季度，我们必须等到看到大幅提升。所以这个时间大约在 3 到 12 个月之间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's really helpful. Okay, so final topic/final question. You've had a truly incredible career. You've worked with incredible companies, incredible leaders. I'm looking at your site here in a site window and you're like, here's a picture of you and Zuck. Here's a picture of you and Toby from Shopify, and there's more. I'm curious what you believe has been key to your success and your career success that you suggest listeners who want to have some measure of similar success do.
turns.zh: 惊人的。这真的很有帮助。好的，最后一个主题/最后一个问题。你的职业生涯确实令人难以置信。您曾与出色的公司、出色的领导者合作过。我在网站窗口中查看您的网站，您会想，这是您和扎克的照片。这是您和 Toby 在 Shopify 上的照片，还有更多内容。我很好奇您认为什么是您成功和职业成功的关键，您建议那些想要获得某种程度类似成功的听众这样做。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: It's probably a bunch of things we could talk about here. Yeah, this is the obvious thing is I think you've just got to love what you do. You got to work hard. You have to have impact. Certainly at the end of the day in growth, that's all that will matter. If I think back to specific things that I do though to pick one thing that's been very important for me throughout my journey is the art of self-reflection. And coaches. I've had coaches my whole career. But the macro theme is you're constantly iterating, experimenting, and becoming the best you can be in your career also as a dad and as a husband, and of course for your own personal health. But that reflection is so important. I've leveraged many, many different coaches over the years and now do a lot of self-reflection through a morning routine that I have and that I've been doing for quite some time that has been a big unlock for me.
turns.zh: 这可能是我们可以在这里讨论的很多事情。是的，这是显而易见的事情，我认为你必须热爱你所做的事情。你必须努力工作。你必须有影响力。当然，归根结底，成长才是最重要的。如果我回想一下我所做的具体事情，我会选择在我的整个旅程中对我来说非常重要的一件事，那就是自我反思的艺术。还有教练。我的整个职业生涯都有教练。但宏观主题是，你不断地迭代、尝试，并成为你职业生涯中最好的人，作为一个父亲和一个丈夫，当然也是为了你自己的个人健康。但这种反思非常重要。多年来，我已经利用了很多很多不同的教练，现在通过我已经做的早上例行工作做了很多自我反思，而且我已经这样做了很长一段时间，这对我来说是一个很大的释放。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: The biggest, most important part of that morning routine is dedicating an hour aside to really think about, "What's going well? What's not going well? What am I screwing up? Well, why am I screwing it up?" Which is often more important than, "What am I screwing up?" And of course, "What am I going to do about it?" But as long as you're learning and iterating every day, then you're just making constant progress towards your goals. It's something I do that I love doing. I love thinking. So I literally can just sit there and think for hours actually. I have a dashboard on all the areas that I'm focusing on with red, yellow, green, and just constantly revving on what am I working on improving, what am I doing, what experiments am I running and where am I doing well and where am I not doing well and how can I be better in all areas of my life, including being a leader. There's a lot of different things to it, but I think that's really important and something that I've learned over the years that is probably the most valuable to have as a skill.
turns.zh: 早上例行公事中最重要、最重要的部分是花一个小时的时间来认真思考，“什么进展顺利？什么进展不顺利？我搞砸了什么？那么，为什么我搞砸了？”这通常比“我搞砸了什么？”更重要。当然，“我该怎么办？”但只要你每天都在学习和迭代，那么你就会朝着你的目标不断进步。这是我喜欢做的事情。我喜欢思考。所以我实际上可以坐在那里思考几个小时。我有一个仪表板，上面标有红色、黄色、绿色的所有我关注的领域，并且不断地加速我正在努力改进什么，我在做什么，我正在进行哪些实验，我在哪里做得好，我在哪里做得不好，以及我如何才能在生活的各个领域变得更好，包括成为领导者。它有很多不同的东西，但我认为这非常重要，也是我多年来学到的东西，这可能是最有价值的技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I definitely want to spend more time on this. So you said you sit for an hour reflecting on what's going well, what's not going well. Is there more you can share about how you accomplish that, how you find time to do this for an hour?
turns.zh: 我绝对想在这上面花更多的时间。所以你说你坐了一个小时反思什么进展顺利，什么进展不顺利。您是否可以分享更多关于您如何实现这一目标，您如何找到时间做一个小时的事情？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, it sounds crazy when you say it, but I do. So I wake up at 5:00. I work out. So I do cardio, I do some exercise. There's this great book called Spark, which is all around the neuroscience of exercise and I really learned a lot from that in terms of having this great morning routine that really boots you up. I kind of call it my bootloader. When I start in the day, if I go through my bootloader, I have just a much better day.
turns.zh: 是的，你这么说听起来很疯狂，但我就是这么做的。所以我在 5:00 起床。我锻炼身体。所以我做有氧运动，做一些运动。有一本很棒的书叫《Spark》，这本书完全围绕运动的神经科学展开，我确实从中学到了很多东西，因为早上的例行公事确实能让你精神焕发。我称之为我的引导加载程序。当我开始新的一天时，如果我通过引导加载程序，我的一天会更好。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So exercise, stretching, meditation, and then I do a cold plunge now. So I do a bunch of different things. But then I do some reading, but I do carve aside one hour where I go through... And this is probably important and it's where I've landed, but structured self reflections. That's why I have this dashboard. I have certain areas that I think about what's going well, what's not. I track all the experiments I'm writing. I'm just really passionate about if you're going to do something, try to do it as best as you can. This is a habit that has allowed me to sharpen my skills in certain areas.
turns.zh: 所以锻炼、伸展身体、冥想，然后我现在会进行一次冷水潜水。所以我做了很多不同的事情。但后来我做了一些阅读，但我确实留出了一个小时来阅读……这可能很重要，这就是我所着陆的地方，但结构化的自我反思。这就是我有这个仪表板的原因。我在某些方面会考虑哪些方面进展顺利，哪些方面进展不佳。我跟踪我正在写的所有实验。我真的很热衷于如果你要做某件事，就尽力做到最好。这个习惯使我能够提高某些领域的技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some of these things you're working on? If you can share what's on this dashboard, how can people imagine what this might be?
turns.zh: 您正在做哪些事情？如果您可以分享此仪表板上的内容，人们怎么能想象这可能是什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So there's a lot of personal stuff on it, but it literally is broken down between being a better friend, better husband, better dad, and then better leader. And so on the personal side, I've been known to work a lot of times. Balance is always hard to find. From being a dad and then thinking about how to be better there, I realized about six months ago that I've never actually asked for feedback on how I'm doing. So I asked my kids six months ago, I asked both of them independently, "What's one thing I can do to do more of or do less of to be a better dad?" And they were kind of caught off guard by it. My son's 15 and my other son is 12. And I said, "Take some time to think about it." And after about a month, my son came back and said, "Dad, I got one." He said, "I want to spend more time with you."
turns.zh: 所以里面有很多个人的东西，但它实际上分为更好的朋友、更好的丈夫、更好的父亲和更好的领导者。因此，就个人而言，我经常工作。平衡总是很难找到。从成为一名父亲，然后思考如何做得更好，大约六个月前，我意识到我从未真正要求过关于我的表现的反馈。所以六个月前我问我的孩子们，我独立地问他们：“为了成为一个更好的父亲，我可以多做或少做哪一件事？”他们对此有点措手不及。我儿子 15 岁，另一个儿子 12 岁。我说：“花点时间考虑一下。”大约一个月后，我儿子回来说：“爸爸，我得到了一个。”他说：“我想和你一起度过更多的时间。”

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So that was very helpful for me to hear. I'm big on routines and habits to make sure that things that you want to do are repeatable and it's not one-off things. So ever since that day, I've now have a daddy date if you want to call it. But every two weeks we do one-on-one time together with each of the boys. They get to pick what we do just so we have that consistent, whether it's dinner or play basketball in the front. But it's all about feedback. So that's one example on the personal side.
turns.zh: 所以这对我来说非常有帮助。我非常注重例程和习惯，以确保你想做的事情是可重复的，而不是一次性的事情。所以从那天起，如果你愿意的话，我现在有一个爸爸约会。但每两周我们都会与每个男孩进行一对一的交流。他们可以选择我们做什么，这样我们就可以保持一致，无论是晚餐还是在前面打篮球。但这一切都与反馈有关。这是个人方面的一个例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of a tweet I just saw where someone said that the only people that are going to remember that you worked late for many nights is your kids.
turns.zh: 这让我想起我刚刚看到的一条推文，有人说，唯一会记得你工作很多晚的人就是你的孩子。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Wow. Wow. That's deep. I like that a lot.
turns.zh: 哇。哇。那很深。我非常喜欢这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a soon to be parent, that's going to stick with me.
turns.zh: 作为一个即将成为父母的人，这一点将永远伴随着我。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Wow, I like that a lot. So it's tough, right? It's tough to balance it all out. It's very difficult because you want excel at everything you do in life. So that reflection helps, be it check-in as well of how am I doing in all these areas? And that I find the color coding is helpful for that too, of just doing a bit of a gut check and asking for that feedback.
turns.zh: 哇，我非常喜欢这个。所以这很难，对吧？很难平衡这一切。这非常困难，因为你想在生活中所做的每一件事上都表现出色。因此，这种反思会有所帮助，无论是检查我在所有这些领域的表现如何？我发现颜色编码对此也很有帮助，只需进行一些内部检查并寻求反馈即可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it also makes me think about, I was watching a Jeff Bezos interview and ask him what his morning routine was and he said that he just likes to putter around. he likes to just sit around, talk to his kids, read the newspaper. He doesn't book any meetings in the morning. He just finds he just needs a little flex time at the beginning.
turns.zh: 所以这也让我想到，我正在观看杰夫·贝佐斯的采访，问他早上的例行公事是什么，他说他只是喜欢闲逛。他喜欢坐下来，和孩子们聊天，看报纸。他没有预订早上的任何会议。他只是发现一开始他只需要一点弹性时间。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Totally. Before I became a dad, I read somewhere that one of the most impactful things you can do as a father is just be there for dinner every night. So I have been there for 15 years every single night. But it was a good reminder it's not enough. Having dinner is important with your family, but in our case there's more you can do. And just getting that feedback and doing some reprioritization is always important.
turns.zh: 完全。在我成为一名父亲之前，我在某处读到，作为一名父亲，你能做的最有影响力的事情之一就是每天晚上在那里吃晚饭。 15年来，我每晚都在那里。但这是一个很好的提醒，但这还不够。与家人共进晚餐很重要，但在我们的情况下，您可以做更多事情。获得反馈并重新调整优先顺序总是很重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of dinners, and maybe just as a last question, I know you do this really interesting thing where you have dinners with interesting people. You just kind of invite them to your house. I don't know if interesting is the right way to describe it, but just kind of interesting people, prominent people. Can you just talk about what that is and what you think about and the benefits of doing something like that?
turns.zh: 说到晚餐，也许作为最后一个问题，我知道你会做一件非常有趣的事情，与有趣的人共进晚餐。你只是邀请他们来你家。我不知道“有趣”是否是描述它的正确方式，但只是一些有趣的人，杰出的人。您能谈谈那是什么、您的想法以及这样做的好处吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I think interesting is the right way to think about it.
turns.zh: 我认为有趣才是正确的思考方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I started this when I was in Ottawa with a bunch of founders there. It's become one of my favorite things to do. Honestly, it's like the bright spot in my month that, I call them guilds. So the word guild is with the builders. That's how it originally started. So Guild Night is what I call it. The idea is basically all interesting people doing interesting things actually want to spend time with each other. That's why I'm actually surprised more people don't do this. But I'll basically have interesting people come, usually five or six. We'll sit around talking about specific topics. So I do one for consumer product, I do one for SEO, I do one for growth leaders and just have really smart, interesting people come and we'll talk about different topics that are relevant.
turns.zh: 当我和一群创始人在渥太华时，我开始了这个工作。这已经成为我最喜欢做的事情之一。老实说，这就像我这个月的亮点，我称之为公会。所以公会这个词与建造者有关。事情最初就是这样开始的。所以我称之为公会之夜。这个想法基本上是所有有趣的人做有趣的事情实际上都想彼此共度时光。这就是为什么我对更多人不这样做感到惊讶。但我基本上会邀请一些有趣的人来，通常是五六个。我们将坐下来讨论特定的话题。因此，我为消费品做了一项，为搜索引擎优化做了一项，为增长领导者做了一项，然后有非常聪明、有趣的人来，我们将讨论相关的不同主题。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Sometimes we'll pick a topic, so we'll have a group and then we'll say, "Hey, we want to talk about AI." So one of the advantages of being in the Bay Area is you can find three or four people that likely wrote some of the core code in Google or in AI, and then they'll join. People want to meet. People want to get together and have these conversations. So it's very exhilarating. I learn a ton. It's a lot of fun. I don't know why more people don't do it. And it's a bit of work to organize, but it's also just tactically been a great way to meet fascinating people. It's helped a lot for recruiting, for if you need a back channel. Now you know all these people that are in different industries. But business aside, they're very valuable business wise, but they're just a lot of fun and they've become some of my favorite things that I do.
turns.zh: 有时我们会选择一个主题，所以我们会组成一个小组，然后我们会说，“嘿，我们想谈论人工智能。”因此，在湾区的优势之一是你可以找到三四个可能在谷歌或人工智能领域编写过一些核心代码的人，然后他们就会加入。人们想要见面。人们希望聚在一起进行这些对话。所以这是非常令人兴奋的。我学到了很多。这很有趣。我不知道为什么更多的人不这样做。组织起来需要一些工作，但从战术上来说，这也是结识有趣的人的好方法。如果您需要后台渠道，这对于招聘有很大帮助。现在你认识了所有这些来自不同行业的人。但撇开商业不谈，它们在商业上非常有价值，而且它们很有趣，而且已经成为我最喜欢做的事情之一。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I'm really surprised why more people don't do it because I think especially now that everybody's remote and we're working from home, or most people are, it's more valued than ever. So it's something I'm looking forward to continuing and always actually through my morning reflection, thinking about what are new ones I can spin up who are interesting people that we want to break bread with. I do think it's important that it's done at your house. If anybody's thinking of starting this, you can do it at a restaurant, but there's something about being in your home or being in somebody's home, five or six people having a great conversation about a topic that's mutually interesting. I think everybody values it and it adds a lot of spice to life. I think it's really important.
turns.zh: 我真的很惊讶为什么更多的人不这样做，因为我认为特别是现在每个人都在远程，我们都在家工作，或者大多数人都是这样，它比以往任何时候都更有价值。所以这是我期待着继续下去的事情，而且总是通过我早上的反思，思考我可以推出哪些新的人，他们是我们想与他们一起分享面包的有趣的人。我确实认为在你家里完成这件事很重要。如果有人想开始这个，你可以在餐馆里做，但是在你家里或在某人家里，五六个人就一个共同感兴趣的话题进行一次愉快的交谈。我认为每个人都重视它，它为生活增添了很多情趣。我认为这非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other tactical tips for making one of these happen? So you do it at your home, you cater. How many people? How long? Anything else you want to share there?
turns.zh: 还有其他战术技巧可以实现其中之一吗？所以你在家里做，你做饭。有多少人？多长时间？您还有什么想在那里分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, so I think the most I've done is 10. That's a bit too much. Six seems to be perfect, six to eight, eight at the max. I do get a catered so you don't have to worry about cooking. The topic, something like a topic that it's common so that everybody can rally around. I do think it's important, like I mentioned, doing it at home. Usually we start around 6:00, we go till 9:00 or 10. It's just been a really good thing that I've learned over time is a really good thing to do to just make for a better life, frankly. Make richer life with some great friends.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我认为我做的最多的是 10 个。这有点太多了。六似乎是完美的，六到八，最多八个。我有包吃的，所以你不用担心做饭。主题，类似于一个常见的主题，以便每个人都可以团结起来。正如我提到的，我确实认为在家做这件事很重要。通常我们在 6:00 左右开始，一直到 9:00 或 10 点。坦率地说，随着时间的推移，我了解到这是一件非常好的事情，可以让生活变得更好。与一些好朋友一起创造更丰富的生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when we say cater, it's just ordering in basically, right? It's not that-
turns.zh: 当我们说餐饮时，基本上只是订购，对吧？不是那个——

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, you can just DoorDash some food so you don't have to worry about cooking. I'm sure there's other things. I've never really deeply thought about it, but in terms of what are the specific things, I've evolved it over time, but I don't cook anyways, so it would be terrible if I cooked. So this is much easier to do it this way. And as long as you're inviting kind of interesting people, everybody's going to want to come and spend some time and bring some bread.
turns.zh: 是的，您可以通过 DoorDash 一些食物，这样您就不必担心烹饪问题。我确信还有其他事情。我从来没有真正深入地思考过，但具体是什么，我随着时间的推移而演变，但我反正不做饭，所以如果我做饭就太糟糕了。所以用这种方法做起来要容易得多。只要你邀请一些有趣的人，每个人都会想来花一些时间并带上一些面包。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好了，至此，我们已经进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I think so.
turns.zh: 我想是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you are. Well, question one. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 我想你是。嗯，问题一。您向其他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So there's one that I've already mentioned, which is Spark. It's the neuroscience of exercise. That's a great book. It's not one of these exercise to stay fit and to live longer. This is really about, frankly, if you exercise and do it in a specific way, they have a kind of blueprint they lay out, it's good for just cognition and kind of horsepower and performance. So that's been a really important one and has been a big part of me building on my morning routine. The second one is when I picked up I think about a year ago or six months, and I recommended it, gee, I don't know, at least to a couple hundred people now because I recommended it to my team. It's called Smart Brevity. Have you heard of this one?
turns.zh: 我已经提到过一个，那就是 Spark。这是运动的神经科学。那是一本很棒的书。这不是保持健康和长寿的运动之一。坦率地说，这实际上是关于如果你锻炼并以特定的方式进行锻炼，他们就会制定出一种蓝图，这对认知、马力和表现都有好处。所以这是非常重要的一件事，也是我建立早晨例行公事的重要组成部分。第二个是当我拿起它时，我想是一年前或六个月前，我推荐了它，哎呀，我不知道，至少现在向几百人推荐了它，因为我向我的团队推荐了它。这就是所谓的“智能简洁”。你听说过这个吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, but I love the sound of it.
turns.zh: 不，但我喜欢它的声音。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I've always been big on writing crisply and being very tight and not having three-page memos that you're sending off. Especially now that we're remote and we're all doing slack and email and different ways of messaging, how tightly you communicate, how crisp your communication is really important for frankly you getting your point across and also for the other person who's probably digesting a hundred of these messages. So this book is... It's a book on how to do that. It breaks down how to write crisply and the different parts of it. I've definitely seen improvements in the team since I've passed around. So that's a great book frankly for anybody, work or personal because we're writing so much and communication is so key. So that's the second one. The third one is a golden oldie. It's one that I've read many, many times and I recommend from a growth perspective. This one youlikely heard of, it's Influence by Cialdini.
turns.zh: 我一直热衷于写作清晰、紧凑，并且没有你发送的三页备忘录。尤其是现在我们处于远程状态，我们都在使用 Slack 和电子邮件以及不同的消息传递方式，您沟通的紧密程度、沟通的清晰程度对于坦率地表达您的观点以及可能正在消化数百条此类消息的其他人来说非常重要。所以这本书是……一本关于如何做到这一点的书。它详细介绍了如何清晰地写作以及其中的不同部分。自从我离开后，我确实看到了团队的进步。坦率地说，这对任何人（无论是工作人员还是个人）来说都是一本很棒的书，因为我们写了很多东西，而沟通非常关键。这是第二个。第三首是金曲。这是我读过很多很多遍的书，我从成长的角度推荐它。您可能听说过这个，它是 Cialdini 的影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got it back on my bookshelf there.
turns.zh: 我把它放回我的书架上。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great book, and it's because it's really the underpinning of so many different product and growth principles that you can apply. So that's just a classic that is good to reread at least once a year. So those are three books.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一本很棒的书，因为它确实是您可以应用的许多不同产品和增长原则的基础。所以这是一部值得每年至少重读一次的经典之作。这是三本书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to extend this a little bit. I'm going to add two books that are building on your two books, or the first two books, I guess. One is Peter Attia just wrote a book called Outlive. That is-
turns.zh: 我将稍微扩展一下。我将添加两本书，这些书是在您的两本书或前两本书的基础上添加的，我猜。其中之一是彼得·阿提亚（Peter Attia）刚刚写了一本名为《Outlive》的书。那是-

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I've got to read it.
turns.zh: 我必须读一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And it's exactly the same kind of premise of just how important exercise is. I think there's a quote in there of just the only thing proven to help you live longer is exercise. And then Smart Brevity, there's another book that I'd recommend if people want more on though on this topic called Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit.
turns.zh: 好的。这与锻炼的重要性完全相同。我认为其中有句话说，唯一被证明可以帮助你长寿的事情就是锻炼。然后，如果人们想了解更多关于这个主题的内容，我会推荐另一本书《Smart Brivity》，名为《没人想读你的狗屎》。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: [inaudible 01:13:08].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's by the guy that wrote the War of Art and Bagger Vance. I forget his name off the top of my head, but it's like, "Nobody wants to read your shit. Here's what you need to do for people to want to read anything you're writing."
turns.zh: 这是《艺术之战》和巴格万斯的作者。我忘记了他的名字，但这就像，“没有人想读你的狗屎。这就是你需要做的事情，让人们想读你写的任何东西。”

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Yeah. We want to scan. We want to read. Yeah, that's great. I'll pick that one up. Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit.
turns.zh: 是的。我们要扫描。我们想读书。是的，那太好了。我会挑选那个。没有人想读你的狗屎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly. What a title.
turns.zh: 确切地。多好的标题啊。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: That's a great title.
turns.zh: 这是一个很棒的标题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, back on track. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 好吧，回到正轨。您最近最喜欢的电影或电视节目是什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I don't watch TV much and I haven't really watched any movies in a while. But I do watch a lot of podcasts on YouTube. Andrew Huberman has got, of course, a great series. I've watched I think everyone he puts out, so I don't know if that counts, but that's-
turns.zh: 我不怎么看电视，也有一段时间没有真正看过电影了。但我确实在 YouTube 上观看了很多播客。当然，安德鲁·胡伯曼有一个很棒的系列。我看过他提出的每个人，所以我不知道这是否重要，但那是-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely
turns.zh: 绝对地

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Okay. So I watched that. And then of course the All-In Podcast is always fun, so I make sure to watch those when they come out as well. A lot of fun and informative. So those are my two, I would say.
turns.zh: 好的。所以我看了那个。当然，All-In 播客总是很有趣，所以我也一定会在它们发布时观看它们。非常有趣且信息丰富。我想说的是，这是我的两个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great picks. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask?
turns.zh: 很棒的选择。您最喜欢问的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Teach me something about growth that I don't already know. Because... and you could apply this to engineering product, any other area, because it really gives you a sense of what this person thinks is the top of the stack in terms of the smartest thing they know. Whether you know it or not is irrelevant. But sometimes you actually do end up learning some stuff. But it's my favorite question because you can really engage in a conversation around, "Okay, the thing you think is so unique that maybe you've come up with this learning yourself or you've created this tactic and then it gives you a sense of how much they know the craft." So that's my favorite question.
turns.zh: 教我一些我还不知道的关于成长的事情。因为……你可以将其应用到工程产品或任何其他领域，因为它确实让你了解这个人认为他们所知道的最聪明的东西是最顶尖的。无论你是否知道，都无关紧要。但有时你实际上最终会学到一些东西。但这是我最喜欢的问题，因为你可以真正参与对话，“好吧，你认为的东西是如此独特，也许你自己想出了这个学习方法，或者你创造了这个策略，然后它让你感觉到他们对这门手艺有多少了解。”这是我最喜欢的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product that you've recently discovered that you just really love?
turns.zh: 您最近发现自己真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I've got a cold plunge that I bought that I love. So it's called the Renew Cold Plunge. It's cold but super convenient and I do that every morning and I just love it.
turns.zh: 我买了一个我喜欢的冷跳水。所以它被称为“更新冷跳”。虽然很冷，但超级方便，我每天早上都会这样做，我非常喜欢它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any advice for cold plunging? That sounds very painful and hard.
turns.zh: 对于冷浸有什么建议吗？这听起来非常痛苦和艰难。

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: I usually start going... I go in a hot tub to warm up, then I go in the cold plunges and back in the hot tub. That's an easy way to get started. But I will say I jumped in yesterday and today without going to hot tub. It was very painful, but I felt so much better after. So I might be changing up my approach, but I'm just kind of experimenting with different things. But that would be some advice. And then just go slow. Start it not too cold, and then slowly make it cold over time. But I think it's a pretty good thing to add in so far.
turns.zh: 我通常会开始......我先进入热水浴缸热身，然后进入冷水池，然后再回到热水浴缸。这是一个简单的入门方法。但我会说我昨天和今天跳了进去，没有去热水浴缸。虽然非常痛苦，但之后我感觉好多了。所以我可能会改变我的方法，但我只是在尝试不同的事情。但这是一些建议。然后慢慢来。开始时不要太冷，然后随着时间的推移慢慢使其变冷。但我认为到目前为止添加进来是一件非常好的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How long have you spent in the cold plunge?
turns.zh: 你在寒冷的环境中度过了多长时间？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: It varies. Right now I'm doing five minutes. Five minutes at, I think it's 53 degrees. So I've started at 60, slowly bringing it down. But you do have to go slow because I brought it down even further and kind of caught me off guard and got a little dizzy. So you got to find your sweet spot.
turns.zh: 它有所不同。现在我正在做五分钟。五分钟后，我认为气温是 53 度。所以我从60岁开始，慢慢降低。但你必须放慢速度，因为我把它放得更远，让我措手不及，有点头晕。所以你必须找到你的最佳位置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Damn. Very Huberman inspired. I imagine this-
turns.zh: 该死。非常受到休伯曼的启发。我想象这个——

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: Definitely it was part of the source there.
turns.zh: 毫无疑问，它是那里的来源的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know people would hear a lot about cold plunges. I guess what have you seen as a benefit just while we're on this topic for people to seriously consider doing this?
turns.zh: 我知道人们会听到很多关于寒流的说法。我想当我们谈论这个话题时，您认为人们认真考虑这样做的好处是什么？

turns.speaker: Luc Levesque
turns.en: So a couple things. Mood afterwards is so much better. You get this great multi-hour boost from doing it. Especially like I mentioned, not doing warm before or waiting 10 minutes and waiting 10 minutes after before you warm up, after you get out, great mood boost. It also helps a lot with sleep. So if you do it at night, which is a little bit difficult, it helps a lot with sleep. Those are probably the two biggest things. And you do get to a point, I'm there now where I kind of look forward to it because you know how good you'll feel afterwards. So when I'm thinking about it, I know it's painful, it doesn't make it easier, but I do look forward to it now. It's a pretty cool thing.
